claude-setup.title: Set up Claude for the first time
claude-setup.subtitle: 15 minutes that improve every future conversation
claude-setup.whatItIs:
15 minutes now save a month of back-and-forth later. Set up your plan, [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]], Memory, Privacy and first Project once — and Claude now knows who you are, what style to answer in, which files to reference. Not a 'generic assistant' — but 'your Claude'.

This tutorial is a mandatory first step for everyone. Without it the other tutorials work 'like for everyone else', not 'like for you'.
claude-setup.approach: Don't skip Privacy settings. Don't write vague Custom Instructions like 'be helpful'. Be specific: your role, your stack, your format preferences. The more concrete, the more Claude adapts.

outcomes.0: Configured Custom Instructions that improve every chat
outcomes.1: Understand Memory — when it helps and when to skip it
outcomes.2: Privacy set according to your preferences
outcomes.3: First Project created with instructions and files
outcomes.4: Know the difference between web, Desktop, and Claude Code

cs-1.title: Choose your plan
cs-1.why: Before configuring anything, confirm you're on the right plan. Free limits hit fast during active use.

instructions.0: Go to claude.ai → click your avatar (top right) → Settings → Account.
instructions.1: Check your current plan: Free / Pro / Team.
instructions.2: Free: limited daily usage, Sonnet/Haiku models only. Pro ($20/mo): Opus access, higher limits, all features.
instructions.3: Rule: use Free for 1 week. If you hit limits daily → upgrade to Pro.

cs-1.validate: You know your current plan and whether it fits your usage.
cs-1.tip: Don't upgrade immediately. Use Free for a week as a diagnostic — you'll know exactly what limits you actually hit.

cs-2.title: Fill in 'About me' (Custom Instructions)
cs-2.why: This tells Claude who you are. Without it, every answer is generic. With it, every answer is tailored to your role.

instructions.0: Settings → Profile → Custom Instructions → 'About me' field.
instructions.1: Write: your role, industry, main tasks, audience, technical stack.
instructions.2: Keep it under 1500 characters. Dense > long.
instructions.3: Avoid: 'I am a kind person'. Write what changes answers: 'I am a senior iOS developer working on fintech apps.'

cs-2.example:
I'm a [role] at [company type], working on [main product/domain].
My main tasks: [task 1], [task 2], [task 3].
Audience for my output: [who reads your work].
Tech stack: [languages, frameworks, tools].
Working language: [language].
cs-2.validate: The field is saved. Open a new chat and ask: 'What do you know about me?' — Claude should reflect your role.
cs-2.tip: The most useful thing to add is your tech stack. Without it, Claude gives generic recommendations.

cs-3.title: Fill in 'How to respond'
cs-3.why: Controls format, tone, length. The difference between needing to rewrite every answer vs using it directly.

instructions.0: Same Settings → Custom Instructions → 'How to respond' field.
instructions.1: Specify: language, format (bullets/prose), length, tone, and what NOT to do.
instructions.2: Save and test on a real task.

cs-3.example:
Always respond in [language].

Format:
- Lead with the key point, then details.
- Use bullet points for lists.
- Max H3 headings — don't over-structure.

Length: exactly what's needed. If 3 sentences work, don't write 10.

Tone: professional but not dry. No filler phrases like 'Great question!'.

Don't:
- Repeat my question back to me.
- Add disclaimers in obvious cases.
- Use emojis unless I start.
cs-3.validate: New chats follow your format and tone without extra prompting.
cs-3.tip: Every time an answer annoys you — add a rule. Your instructions improve through real use.

cs-4.title: Configure Memory
cs-4.why: Memory lets Claude remember facts across conversations. Useful for recurring context — but not a replacement for Custom Instructions.

instructions.0: Settings → Profile → Memory (if available on your plan).
instructions.1: Enable Memory if you want Claude to remember things you tell it across sessions.
instructions.2: You can view and delete what Claude remembers at any time.
instructions.3: Note: Memory works in claude.ai chats. For Claude Desktop, memory is available via MCP memory server.

cs-4.validate: You know whether Memory is on or off and understand what it stores.
cs-4.tip: Memory is additive — Claude stores things you mention. It won't override your Custom Instructions. Think of it as a sticky notepad.

cs-5.title: Set Privacy settings
cs-5.why: By default, Anthropic may use your conversations to improve models. If you work with sensitive data, opt out.

instructions.0: Settings → Privacy.
instructions.1: Find 'Improve Claude for everyone' or similar training data option.
instructions.2: Toggle OFF if you don't want your conversations used for model training.
instructions.3: Pro and Team plans have stronger privacy defaults than Free.

cs-5.validate: Privacy setting matches your preference. You know what data Anthropic stores.
cs-5.tip: This doesn't affect Claude's quality for you — it only affects whether Anthropic uses your data for future training.

cs-6.title: Create your first Project
cs-6.why: Projects give Claude persistent context, files, and specialized instructions for a specific domain of work. Better than repeating context every chat.

instructions.0: In the left sidebar → click 'New Project'.
instructions.1: Name it by domain: 'Work', 'Coding', 'Writing', etc.
instructions.2: Add Project Instructions: paste a specialized version of your Custom Instructions for this domain.
instructions.3: Upload 1-3 reference files if relevant (style guide, codebase docs, templates).
instructions.4: Open a chat inside the Project — Claude now operates in this specialized context.

cs-6.example:
Project: 'Code Review'
Instructions: You are a senior code reviewer for our React/TypeScript codebase. Focus on: type safety, component reusability, performance. Flag: any direct DOM manipulation, missing error boundaries, unhandled promises. Format: bullet list by severity (Critical / Warning / Info).
cs-6.validate: Project created with instructions. Test: ask 'who are you?' inside the Project — Claude should describe the specialized role.
cs-6.tip: Don't create a project for every task. Start with 1-2 that match your most frequent work contexts.

claude-setup.trigger: First week with Claude — or rebuilding your profile after a role/task change.
inputs: Description of your work: role, task types, tools
List of private contexts for Memory (optional)
outputs: Custom Instructions tailored to your role
Memory enabled with baseline context
A first Project with the right structure

basics.title: Master the basics of Claude
basics.subtitle: Models, context, system prompt — in practice
basics.whatItIs:
Which Claude model to pick? Opus = your top expert for hard work (strategy, parsing dense PDFs). Sonnet = everyday workhorse (90% of tasks, balance of price and quality). Haiku = lightning-fast for the simple stuff (classification, short answers).

Plus the key concepts: what the [[node:b-context|context window]] is and why AI "forgets" the start of a long conversation, what a [[node:b-system|system prompt]] is and how it changes Claude's behavior. Without this foundation, the other tutorials are just a list of instructions without understanding.
basics.approach: Don't try to memorize theory — go through the steps in Claude and compare answers with your own eyes. Knowledge from practice sticks 10× longer than from an article.
outcomes: You consciously choose a model for the task
You write a structured prompt in 30 seconds
You know when the context has gone stale and a new chat is needed
You know the typical scenarios where Claude makes mistakes

applyIn.title: Daily work
applyIn.description: Any work request to Claude now goes through a structured prompt — that's a free +30% quality boost.

applyIn.title: Model selection
applyIn.description: Before a big task — ask yourself: Opus, Sonnet, or Haiku? The right choice saves tokens and time.

applyIn.title: Long conversations
applyIn.description: You notice the model getting confused — open a new chat and bring over only the key conclusions.

pitfalls: Studying theory from articles without practice — it won't stick.
Using one model for everything — either slow/expensive, or shallow.
Dumping 50 files 'just in case' — the model loses focus.

exercises.question: Take a real work task and write a prompt using the schema 'Role → Task → Format → Constraints'. Send it to Sonnet.
exercises.hint: If you get a generic answer — check whether you explicitly stated the constraints and format.

exercises.question: Rewrite your typical one-liner request as a structured prompt. Compare the answers.
exercises.hint: The contrast should be noticeable — the structured version is usually 2× more detailed.

s1.title: Sign in to Claude.ai and set up your workspace
s1.why: This is the entry point — without an account you can't compare models or feel the difference.
instructions: Open [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] in Chrome or Safari (Firefox works too).
Sign in or register. The Free plan is enough for first steps; Pro is needed for Opus and Projects.
Close the onboarding pop-ups — we'll learn structurally, not through tips.
s1.validate: You see the 'Reply to Claude…' field and a sidebar with chat history on the left.

troubleshoot.Phone verification requested: This is normal — Anthropic blocks bots. Enter a real number.
troubleshoot.Can't find the model selector: The model button is above the input field or in the top-right corner of the chat.

s2.title: Compare Haiku, Sonnet and Opus on the same task
s2.why: Without comparison you won't pick the right model for a task — you'll either overpay or lose depth.
instructions: Create 3 chats (one per model: Haiku → Sonnet → Opus).
Send the same prompt below to each — WITHOUT changes.
Compare the answers by: length, specificity, nuance, generation speed.
Note down: which model 'hit' the task best.
s2.prompt:
Explain why two equally talented junior developers can produce radically different results in the same team.

Give 5 reasons, rank by impact, and for each explain the mechanism. No fluff and no obvious 'communication is important'.
s2.validate: You have 3 chats with the same prompt and three answers of different depth.
s2.tip: Haiku is good for drafts and simple tasks, Sonnet is for everyday work, Opus is for complex reasoning and audits.

troubleshoot.Opus not available: Pro/Team only. If on Free — use Sonnet, it's close to Opus for most tasks.

s3.title: Feel the power of a system prompt
s3.why: Without a role the model answers like Wikipedia. With a role — like an expert on your task. Quality difference is 30–50%.
instructions: Open a new Sonnet chat.
Send the 'naive' prompt (see the block below).
Open a second chat, send the 'prompt with role'.
Compare: how much more concrete the second answer is, tied to constraints, without fluff.
s3.prompt:
[NAIVE PROMPT — send as-is]
How can I improve my project?

[PROMPT WITH ROLE — send in the second chat]
You are an expert in my domain with a focus on practical results.
Context: describe your task, audience, environment (1–2 sentences).
Task: give 5 recommendations for improving <your object — page / report / process>.
Format: problem → why it hurts the result → what to do.
Constraint: only things that can be implemented in a week without outside help.
s3.validate: The second answer is specific, tied to constraints, without generic phrases.
s3.tip: Memorize the structure: context → role → task → format → constraints. That's 80% of a good prompt.

s4.title: See how the context window works
s4.why: Understanding the context limit saves you from 'hallucinations' and quality loss on long conversations.
instructions: In one chat, ask Claude to briefly introduce itself (see below).
In the same chat, ask 5–7 unrelated questions in a row.
Then ask: 'What was the very first question I asked after your introduction?' — Claude should remember.
This shows that the whole chat is one shared context, not a series of independent requests.
s4.prompt: Introduce yourself in one line. After that I'll ask several different questions.
s4.validate: For the last question Claude correctly quotes the first.
s4.tip: When a chat goes stale (the model gets confused) — open a new one and bring over only the essentials. Don't drag garbage into the context.

s5.title: Refine the answer iteratively instead of rewriting from scratch
s5.why: Beginners ditch the first answer and write a brand-new prompt. But Claude remembers the whole chat — a targeted tweak ('make it shorter', 'add an example', 'drop point 3') is faster and more precise than starting over.
instructions: Take any answer from the previous steps that was 'almost, but not quite' right.
Don't start a new chat — write one short follow-up right in the same conversation (e.g. 'too generic, give concrete steps' or 'cut it in half and keep only points 1 and 4').
Once you get the new version, refine it again with a single phrase about what to fix.
Notice: with each iteration the answer gets closer, because Claude keeps the full edit history in context.
s5.prompt: Too generic. Rewrite it for my situation: <1 sentence about your context>. Keep only concrete actions, no intro.
s5.validate: You got the answer to where you needed it in 2–3 short follow-ups, without rewriting the original prompt.
s5.tip: One follow-up = one change. If you ask for five edits at once, the model drops some. Refine step by step.

s6.title: Lock it in: pick a model for your real task
s6.why: Without applying it to your own task, the learning stays theory.
instructions: Take YOUR actual task for this week.
Ask yourself: which model is optimal (Haiku / Sonnet / Opus)?
What role and format are needed in the system prompt?
Launch the task right now — while it's fresh.
s6.validate: You have a running chat with YOUR task and a conscious choice of model + role.
s6.tip: Continue developing this in 'Prompt Engineering' — we'll go deeper into techniques there.

projects.title: Create your first Project
projects.subtitle: A long-lived workspace with its own context
projects.whatItIs:
You have 5 recurring tasks every week (content, audits, reviews)? Each time you re-explain context to Claude from scratch? A Project turns Claude into a specialist for that specific task — set up once, remembered always.

A Project is a 'folder' in [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] with its own instructions and knowledge base files. Every chat inside knows the context without re-briefing.
projects.approach: The key is to choose ONE recurring task for the first Project. Not 'everything about work' — something specific. Narrow focus = high quality.
outcomes: Create a Project for a recurring task
Write [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]] that change answer quality
Upload the right materials to Project Knowledge
Know when a Project is needed and when a regular chat is enough

applyIn.title: Regular audits
applyIn.description: A Project with guides and cases — every week you review new material against the same criteria.

applyIn.title: Template documents
applyIn.description: Templates and examples in Knowledge → Claude drafts in your style, you refine.

applyIn.title: Onboarding a new hire
applyIn.description: Share the Project — a new employee immediately gets a 'specialized' Claude for the project.

pitfalls: Making one Project for everything. Better 3–5 narrow ones than one universal.
Uploading everything into Knowledge — the model loses focus on irrelevant content.
Writing instructions like 'be helpful' — that's noise, not a rule.

exercises.question: Write down your 3 recurring tasks. For the most frequent one — create a Project with minimal instructions and 1–2 files.
exercises.hint: Recurring = repeats ≥ once a week with a similar process.

exercises.question: Run your next real task through this Project. Compare with how you did it in a regular chat.
exercises.hint: If you see no difference — the instructions are weak; refine them based on results.

s1.title: Open Projects and create one with a name
s1.why: Projects are only available on paid plans — without one the next steps are impossible. And a meaningful name becomes an anchor: 'Project 1' you won't remember in 2 weeks; 'Regular Report Audit' you will.
instructions: Go to claude.ai → top-right corner → check your subscription. If Free — upgrade to Pro ($20/month) or use a team account.
In the left sidebar find 'Projects' → '+ New project'.
Name: '<what we do> <for whom / what>'. E.g., 'Regular Report Audit' or 'Client Meeting Prep'.

Description: 1–2 lines — what the project is for, who will work in it, what result is expected. Example: 'We come here before each iteration to prepare/review results. Core materials and templates are here.'
Click Create.
If you don't see a Projects section — are you sure you have Pro? Sometimes you need to log out and back in after an upgrade.
s1.validate: Project created, you see an empty chat and the 'Project knowledge' / 'Instructions' panel.
s1.tip: Don't make one Project for everything. Better 3–5 specialized ones than one universal.

s2.title: Write Custom Instructions
s2.why: This is the highest-ROI time investment in the Project. Without instructions — a folder with files; with them — a specialized assistant.
instructions: Open the Project panel → Custom instructions.

Use the framework below, filling in your domain:

You are a [role] with [N] years of experience in [niche].

Work context:
- Task type: [the main thing we do]
- Audience for results: [who will read]
- Team style: [how we communicate, format]

Answer format:
- Key point first, then details
- Bullet lists for enumerations
- For recommendations: problem → impact → what to do
- Length: exactly what's needed — no fluff

What you do NOT do:
- Don't give generic advice without grounding in context
- Don't suggest solutions that require resources we don't have
- Don't mix languages unnecessarily
Save. All future chats in this Project will automatically pick up the instructions.
s2.validate: After saving, send 'who are you?' — Claude should answer as the assigned role, not a generic assistant.
s2.tip: The most common mistake — overly generic instructions like 'be helpful'. That's noise. Specificity > politeness.

s3.title: Upload key files to Project knowledge
s3.why: Files become 'permanent memory' — Claude sees them in all Project chats, no need to repeat context.
instructions: In the right Project panel → Project knowledge → Add content / Upload.
Upload 3–7 KEY documents: brand guide, brief, guidelines, reference cases.
Don't upload everything — 5 precise ones beat 50 random ones. Each extra file dilutes focus.
Give each file a clear name — Claude uses it for navigation.
If a file is too large — the limit is usually 30 MB per file; compress images or split the PDF. For long PDFs, extract the key sections into a separate markdown.
s3.validate: You see the list of uploaded files in Project knowledge with a 'ready' checkmark.
s3.tip: Less noise, higher accuracy: 5 precise documents work better than 50 random ones.

s4.title: Run the first real request
s4.why: Without a real test the Project is just a hypothesis. The request will show how well the instructions and files are tuned.
instructions: In the Project open a new chat.

Send the prompt (adapt it to your task): 'Using the materials from knowledge: do your regular task for the input data — [URL / document / description]. Give the result in the format described in the instructions.'
Evaluate: did Claude answer in the right format, did it use the uploaded files.
s4.validate: The answer is in the format from the instructions, with explicit references to the uploaded files.
s4.tip: If Claude doesn't use knowledge — ask explicitly: 'rely on the materials from Project knowledge'.

s5.title: Iterate the instructions based on results
s5.why: The first Project is rarely perfect. Real conversations show what needs tightening in the instructions.
instructions: After 2–3 chats write down: what does Claude do wrong?

Rephrase each 'wrong' as a rule and add it to Custom instructions. Example: BEFORE — long fluffy answers; AFTER — 'Never write openers like 'great question'. Get straight to the point.' BEFORE — generic advice not tied to our stack; AFTER — 'All recommendations — only within the Next.js + Tailwind stack described in knowledge.'
Save. New chats will immediately apply the changes.
s5.validate: [[node:instructions|Custom instructions]] grew by 3–5 rules, each born from a real problem.
s5.tip: A Project is a living document. 10 minutes of instruction review every month saves hours of routine.

s6.title: Share with the team (if Team plan)
s6.why: One Project for the team = one quality standard. Everyone stops 'inventing their own Claude'.
instructions: Open the Project → Share → Add team members.
Choose access level: Editor (can change instructions) / Viewer (read chats only).
Pin the Project in the team wiki / Notion with a short note: 'when and how to use it'.
s6.validate: Colleagues see the Project in their lists and can open chats.
s6.tip: Designate one 'Project curator' — they own the cleanliness of instructions and knowledge. Without a curator the Project degrades within a month.

artifacts.title: Create your first interactive Artifact
artifacts.subtitle: A prototype you can open, click around, and rebuild
artifacts.whatItIs:
You asked Claude for an HTML landing page prototype — it opens in a separate window next to the chat, you can see how it looks and immediately say 'make the button greener'. No copy-pasting to an editor and back. That's an Artifact.

A separate 'canvas' in [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] for code, HTML, SVG, documents. Runnable preview right in the browser, iterations with version history, no walls of text in chat.
artifacts.approach: Don't try to 'draw' a perfect final version in the Artifact right away. It's an iteration tool — 3–5 cycles of 'get → poke → rewrite' produce a better result than '10 pages of requirements upfront'.
outcomes: You trigger an Artifact intentionally — not by accident
You build interactive HTML prototypes in minutes
You use versions for safe iteration
You share an Artifact with a public link to colleagues

applyIn.title: Idea prototype
applyIn.description: A page / screen concept assembled in 10 minutes in HTML+Tailwind, a live link sent to the team — we discuss the real thing, not a description.

applyIn.title: A shareable document
applyIn.description: A report / guide / meeting summary formatted as an Artifact — it can be opened and read as a standalone document.

applyIn.title: Micro-utility
applyIn.description: A calculator / converter / visualization — assembled in 15 minutes, runs in the browser without a backend.

pitfalls: Not specifying the format — Claude will put the code in the chat instead of an Artifact.
Asking for 'everything at once' — iterations are more effective.
Ignoring versions — you lose good intermediate results.

exercises.question: Describe to Claude a prototype of one page for your project. Get the Artifact. Revise it 2–3 times.
exercises.hint: Change ONE thing each time — this shows the power of iteration.

exercises.question: Rewrite your last Word/Notion documentation as a Markdown Artifact with a table of contents.
exercises.hint: You'll get a standalone document that's more pleasant to read than in the chat.

s1.title: Understand when an Artifact is triggered
s1.why: An Artifact is the 'product' of the work (code / HTML / SVG / Markdown). Not knowing how to trigger it means you keep getting walls of text in the chat.
instructions: An artifact is triggered automatically for: code longer than ~20 lines, HTML/React, SVG, Mermaid, long documents.
You can explicitly ask: 'put this in an Artifact'.
The right preview panel opens — it shows the code AND the visual result.
s1.validate: You understand that an Artifact is a separate panel, not text in the chat.
s1.tip: If Claude put a large block of code in the chat — ask: 'move this into an Artifact'. It will.

s2.title: Request the first HTML prototype
s2.why: A prototype in an Artifact is the fastest way to see an idea 'live' instead of a verbal description.
instructions: Open a new chat (can be inside a Project).
Copy the prompt below, substitute your topic.
Wait for generation — a preview opens on the right.
Click 'Preview' / 'Code' — switch between the visual and the code.
s2.prompt:
Build an interactive single-file HTML prototype as an Artifact.

What we're building: a subscription pricing page with three tiers and a month/year toggle.
Audience: SaaS B2B.
Stack: plain HTML + Tailwind via CDN. No React. No third-party dependencies.

Requirements:
- mobile-first, correct down to 320px
- accessible semantics (label, aria-*)
- 3 states: idle, loading, success
- meaningful copy instead of lorem ipsum

Show the preview immediately.
s2.validate: You see a preview with three tiers and a toggle; everything works in the preview window.
s2.tip: If the preview breaks — ask 'fix the preview, I'm getting a blank screen'. Claude will find the bug.

s3.title: Make a targeted edit
s3.why: A targeted edit saves tokens and doesn't break the working parts. This is the main way to iterate.
instructions: In the chat with the Artifact, ask to change ONE specific thing.
Don't use 'improve everything' — Claude will rewrite half randomly.
Wait for the new version — 'Version 2' will appear at the top of the Artifact.
s3.prompt: In this Artifact change the primary color to #0F172A. Don't touch the font in the other sections. Make the buttons slightly larger (py-3 → py-4).
s3.validate: Version 2 contains exactly those three changes; everything else is identical.
s3.tip: The more precisely you state the edit, the fewer unwanted changes. Compare: 'make it prettier' ❌ vs 'change the radius from 8 to 12, leave everything else' ✅

s4.title: Use versions for safe experiments
s4.why: Versioning removes the fear of iteration. Doesn't work — roll back.
instructions: Ask Claude to radically rework a section (see prompt).
Get version 3.
At the top of the Artifact click the versions dropdown — switch back to version 2.
Confirm that the previous work is not lost.
s4.prompt: Now make an experimental alternative: a hero section with a large emotional headline and a video background instead of the gradient. Completely redraw the top of the page.
s4.validate: You have at least 3 Artifact versions and switching between them works.
s4.tip: Before experiments, save the version you liked to Notion / GitHub — just in case.

s5.title: Finalize and take the code
s5.why: Without moving to a repository, the Artifact stays a demo. This step takes it to real production.
instructions: When you're happy with the version — click 'Copy' in the top-right corner of the Artifact.
Paste into your project (a separate file or component).
If the code is React — ask Claude to split it into separate files: 'give me these components as a file structure'.
s5.validate: Code is pasted into your project and builds without errors.
s5.tip: Don't copy everything at once. Before copying, ask Claude: 'go through the code and remove unnecessary comments and commented-out junk'.

s6.title: Publish the Artifact and share the link
s6.why: An Artifact stays private until you publish it. Publishing turns it into a live page a colleague opens in their browser without access to your chat — better than a screenshot and faster than deploying a project.
instructions: Get the right version to a presentable state (real copy instead of placeholders, no broken preview).
Click 'Publish' / 'Share' in the top-right corner of the Artifact and confirm publication.
Copy the public link and send it to a colleague — they open the interactive result without joining your conversation.
When the draft is no longer needed — Unpublish it so the link stops working.
s6.validate: Open the public link in an incognito window (no account) — the Artifact is visible and interactive.
s6.tip: The public link exposes only the artifact itself, not the chat history. Still check: no private key, token, or internal URL is baked into the code — exactly what's inside gets published.

artifacts.trigger: You need to show a live prototype, landing or diagram — not static text.
outputs: Interactive artifact in the side panel
"Make it greener / add a block" iteration with no copy-paste
Ready HTML/code to share
artifacts.savings: ~1-2 hours per prototype vs manual coding in an editor

instructions.title: Configure Custom Instructions
instructions.subtitle: Make Claude 'yours' at the profile level
instructions.whatItIs:
Tired of explaining to Claude every time "I'm in marketing, answer briefly in English, no fluff"? [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]] is the field in your [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] profile where it's written once. Applies to ALL chats automatically.

Two fields: 'About me' (who you are) and 'How to respond' (how to answer). Fill them once — every Claude response now factors in your role, style, and constraints. Base investment: 5 minutes now, payoff forever.
instructions.approach: Fill them concisely, not at length — length doesn't equal quality. The most useful things: your role/industry/stack + 3–5 rules like 'don't give disclaimers in obvious cases'. Every time an answer annoys you — add a rule.

outcomes.0: Know the difference between global and Project instructions
outcomes.1: Filled in 'About me' so that answers actually change
outcomes.2: Described the format and tone in 'How to respond'
outcomes.3: Can iterate instructions based on real conversation results

0.title: Quality from the first message
0.description: Without instructions every chat starts with a briefing. With them — Claude is already 'specialized' for you.

1.title: Consistent format across the team

s1.title: Open profile settings
s1.why: Custom Instructions at the profile level apply to ALL chats — this is the baseline investment.

instructions.0: In claude.ai → click the avatar (top right) → Settings.
instructions.1: Find the 'Profile' / 'Custom Instructions' section.
instructions.2: You see two fields: 'About me' and 'How to respond'.

s1.validate: You see a form with two text fields.

troubleshoot.Can't see Settings: Sometimes the section is called Preferences. Or it's hidden behind '···'. Look carefully.

s2.title: Fill in 'About me'
s2.why: This is context about you. Without it Claude answers 'for everyone'; with it — for exactly your role.

instructions.0: Describe: role, experience, domain, main tasks, audience for your work.
instructions.1: Don't write 'I'm a good person'. Write what changes Claude's answers.
instructions.2: Length — up to 1500 characters. Density > length.

s2.example:
<Describe your role in one line: title + industry + context.>
<Your experience: years, key strengths.>
Audience for my output: <who you exchange results with>.

I regularly work with:
- <your regular task #1>
- <your regular task #2>
- <your regular task #3>

<If relevant — your tech stack / tools / systems.>
Working language: <language / languages you work in>.
s2.validate: 'About me' is filled in, describing things that change the answers (role, domain, stack, work format).
s2.tip: The most useful thing to add is a specific stack/tools. Without them, Claude recommends generically.

s3.title: Fill in 'How to respond'
s3.why: This field controls style and format. It determines how much you can use answers without editing.

instructions.0: Describe: language, length, format, tone, what NOT to do.
instructions.1: Use the template below — it covers 90% of cases.
instructions.2: Save and test on a typical task.

s3.example:
Always respond in [language]. Technical terms — don't translate if the translation is awkward.

Format:
- Key point first, then details.
- Bullet lists for enumerations.
- H3 headings max, don't over-structure.

Length: exactly what's needed. If you can say it in 3 sentences — don't write 10.

Tone: professional, not stiff. But not dry either — some irony is fine where appropriate.

Do NOT:
- Write openers like 'Great question!'
- Repeat my request back to me.
- Use emojis in body text (unless I start).
- Give 'consult an expert' disclaimers in obvious cases.
s3.validate: The field is saved; new chats follow your format and tone.
s3.tip: If something still annoys you in the answers — that's a signal to add a new rule.

s4.title: Remove vague wording
s4.why: A vague rule like 'write well' gets ignored — the model doesn't know what 'well' means to you. A concrete, observable rule changes the answer; a fuzzy one doesn't.

instructions.0: Reread your instructions and underline abstract words: 'quality', 'professional', 'clear', 'friendly'.
instructions.1: Replace each one with observable behavior: 'clear' → 'no jargon; explain a term in parentheses on first use'.
instructions.2: Delete rules Claude already follows by default — they only add noise to the instruction.
instructions.3: Check rule: if you can't tell unambiguously whether a line was followed or not, rewrite it.

s4.example:
Before (vague):
- Write with quality and professionalism.
- Be friendly.
- Explain clearly.

After (observable):
- Back every claim with an example or a number.
- Business tone; no 'hi!', no 'hope this helps'.
- Explain a term in parentheses (one word) on first use.
s4.validate: No abstract judgments remain in the instructions — only rules where it's visible whether they were followed.
s4.tip: Vagueness test: give two wordings to a colleague and ask 'how would you check this?'. If they can't, Claude can't either.

s5.title: Test run on 3 different tasks
s5.why: Without testing, instructions may 'not kick in'. The test is your mirror.

instructions.0: Open 3 new chats and set 3 different tasks (everyday, professional, creative).
instructions.1: Check: does each answer match the instructions.
instructions.2: Where it doesn't — write down and refine the instructions.

s5.example:
Test 1: a technical task — example from your domain
Test 2: a professional task — example from your domain
Test 3: a creative task — example from your domain
s5.validate: All three answers are in the right language, format, tone.
s5.tip: A checklist of rules born from real problems = the best kind of instructions. Don't write 'be friendly' — write 'don't use the word disclaimer'.

s6.title: Adapt at the Project level (if you have one)
s6.why: [[node:p-instructions|Project instructions]] override global ones. Each niche gets its own specialized set.

instructions.0: Open your Project → Custom Instructions.
instructions.1: Here add only what is specific to the Project's NICHE.
instructions.2: Global rules (language, format) are already inherited — don't duplicate.

s6.example:
[In Project '<your regular task>']

In addition to my global instructions:

In this Project you are a specialist in my domain with a specific focus (describe).

Format of each result:
1. Context / input data
2. Problem or principle that was violated
3. Impact (high / medium / low)
4. Recommendation (concrete action, not an abstraction)

Draw on the materials from Project knowledge.
s6.validate: The Project works in a specialized mode; global rules are not broken.
s6.tip: Test: ask in the Project 'who are you?'. It should answer as the specialized role, not a generic assistant.

instructions.trigger: You explain "I work in marketing, answer in English, no fluff" in every new chat.
outputs: Filled About me / Response style fields
Auto-applied to all chats
Template shareable with the team
instructions.savings: ~2-3 min per new chat — ~1 hour/week net

prompting.title: Level up your prompt engineering
prompting.subtitle: Turn 'I asked' into 'I got predictable quality'
prompting.whatItIs:
Same request to Claude — one gives a hollow 'here's a general overview of the topic...', another gives a concrete plan with numbers. The only difference is the wording. That's prompt engineering — the skill of 'how to ask so AI answers usefully'.

Five levers: structure, context, examples, role, constraints. Same AI, results 5-10× apart — all the difference is in how you phrase the request.
prompting.approach: Don't study techniques from a list. Take your REAL weak prompt and upgrade it step by step. Each step = +one technique. By the end of the tutorial this prompt works 3–5× better — and you understand why.
outcomes: You write prompts using the schema context → role → task → format → constraints
You use XML tags to separate instructions from data
You apply few-shot when the model doesn't catch the pattern
You enable Chain of Thought on analytical tasks

applyIn.title: Any non-trivial task
applyIn.description: Before a complex request — 30 seconds on structure. The cheapest way to raise quality.

applyIn.title: Analytical tasks
applyIn.description: Comparisons, assessments, conclusions — always with Chain of Thought or Tree of Thought.

applyIn.title: Reproducible formats
applyIn.description: If the result needs to be in JSON/table — describe the schema explicitly and give 1–2 examples.

pitfalls: A one-liner 'do it well' — the most common source of bad answers.
Too many few-shot examples — the model 'confuses' patterns.
CoT on simple tasks — just extra noise.

exercises.question: Find your weak prompt from history. Rewrite it using the full schema (role/context/task/format/constraints). Compare answers.
exercises.hint: The worse the original prompt — the more noticeable the upgrade effect.

exercises.question: Take a complex analytical task. Do it TWICE: without CoT and with a CoT trigger. Measure the difference.
exercises.hint: CoT trigger: 'Think step by step before answering' at the end of the prompt.

s1.title: Take your real prompt
s1.why: Learning on your own tasks is 10× more effective than on synthetic ones. Find yours.
instructions: Find in the chat history a prompt that Claude answered 'not great'.
Copy it into notes — we'll upgrade it step by step.
Write down what in the answer you did NOT like (vague? generic? wrong format?).
Example. My prompt: 'Help me improve my project'. What I didn't like: the answer — generic textbook advice. Not tied to my product, audience, or tools.
s1.validate: You have a real 'weak' prompt in hand and a list of complaints about the answer.
s1.tip: The worse the prompt — the more noticeable the upgrade. Don't pick a good one — pick a typical one.

s2.title: Apply the basic structure
s2.why: The structure 'context → role → task → format → constraints' solves 80% of weak-prompt problems.
instructions: Rewrite your prompt using the template below.
Fill in all fields — missing ones = weak spots.
Send to Claude and compare with the previous answer.

Template:
[CONTEXT]
<Briefly describe your project, audience, current stage (1–2 sentences).>

[ROLE]
You are an expert in my domain with a specific focus (describe).

[TASK]
Give 5 recommendations for <your object>. Input data: [URL / document / description].

[FORMAT]
For each problem:
- what's wrong (1 line)
- impact (high / medium / low)
- what to do (concrete action, not abstraction)

[CONSTRAINTS]
- Only things that can be implemented within <realistic timeframe>
- No recommendations requiring a fundamental rewrite
- Draw on proven principles / standards in your domain
s2.validate: The answer is specific, tied to context, in the right format.
s2.tip: If even one field is empty — fill it in. Each field improves answer accuracy.

s3.title: Add XML tags for long prompts
s3.why: XML markup separates instructions from data. Claude is trained on it — understands it perfectly.
instructions: If the prompt contains data / examples / code — wrap them in XML tags.
Use meaningful tag names: <context>, <task>, <example>, <code>.
This is especially important when instructions and data could get mixed up.

Example:
<context>
<Brief description of the task and domain.>
</context>

<input_data>
[all the material here — text, description, code or other inputs]
</input_data>

<task>
Find the critical problems in this material.
</task>

<format>
- problem
- impact
- recommendation
</format>
s3.validate: The prompt reads clearly: where are the instructions, where is the data.
s3.tip: XML is for long prompts with data. For short ones — overkill.

s4.title: Give a few-shot example
s4.why: 'Input → output' examples are stronger than any description. This is the most underrated technique.
instructions: Give 1–3 examples: what input → what output.
Examples — for the SAME type of task as the real request.
After the examples — your real request.

Example:
<example>
Input: "SaaS login form"
Output:
- Problem: 6 fields including password repeat and captcha — that causes 30% drop-off at this step.
- Impact: high — this is a critical funnel point.
- Recommendation: remove captcha (show only on suspicion), remove 'repeat password' (there's a 'show password' option).
</example>

<example>
Input: "SaaS landing hero section"
Output:
- Problem: headline 'Business Solution' — generic, doesn't explain the value.
- Impact: high — the user doesn't understand what the product is.
- Recommendation: rewrite in the format '<verb> <result> <in time>' — e.g., 'Track your team's work hours in 5 minutes a day'.
</example>

Now do the same for my material: [URL / document / description]
s4.validate: The answer is in exactly the same format as the examples. The style is copied.
s4.tip: 2 examples are stronger than 5. Too many examples — the model 'confuses' patterns.

s5.title: Add Chain of Thought (for analytical tasks)
s5.why: CoT improves accuracy on complex tasks by 1.2–1.4×. For simple ones — just extra noise.
instructions: If the task requires REASONING (not 'extract a fact'), add a CoT trigger.
Simple trigger: 'Think step by step before answering'.
Advanced: give explicit reasoning steps.

Example:
Task: evaluate which of three architectures is faster for our use case.

Think step by step before answering:
1. Write out my load parameters (RPS, request size, write frequency).
2. For each architecture — where is the bottleneck under this load.
3. Which architecture is easier to scale vertically / horizontally.
4. Only then — the recommendation and justification.
s5.validate: The answer shows the reasoning process, then the final recommendation.
s5.tip: Don't use CoT for creative or short tasks — it'll be a 'parody of reasoning'.

s6.title: Compare 'before/after' and save as a template
s6.why: Without an explicit comparison you won't feel the effect — and won't lock in the skill. And one tuned prompt = a template you'll use hundreds of times. Don't lose it.
instructions: Run the original 'weak' prompt in a new chat.
Run the improved one in another.
Put them side by side. Note: length doesn't matter, accuracy and usability do.
Replace specific values with placeholders [...] (product, link, audience).
Save the improved version as a template in your library (Notion, text file, snippets).
Use it every time — don't write from scratch.
s6.validate: A clear qualitative difference is visible: the improved version is usable without editing, the original isn't. The template is in your library; you can apply it in 30 seconds.
s6.tip: Copy prompt templates into Notion / your 'prompt-library' repository. In a year that's your main asset. Next — the 'Ready prompts' section in the map: 10 templates for typical tasks.

ready-prompts.title: Use ready-made prompts
ready-prompts.subtitle: The fastest way to get quality
ready-prompts.whatItIs: Ready-made prompts are parameterized templates for typical tasks. Open, fill in your data, send — get a structured answer. The fastest way to get quality without learning prompt engineering. And then you fine-tune the template for yourself and turn it into a personal, reusable asset.
ready-prompts.approach: Don't try to write your own prompts from scratch until you've mastered the ready-made ones. Every time you see a typical task — look for a template first, then think. 80% of work is solved by the ready-made. The remaining 20% is your adaptation, worth saving and reusing.
outcomes: Open the ready-made prompt library with one click
Find the right template via search or category filter
Adapt a parameterized template to your case in a minute
Fine-tune the prompt to your style and response requirements
Save and reuse your favorite templates

pitfalls: Using a template without filling in the parameters — Claude answers the literal placeholder.
Not saving adapted versions as bookmarks — you start from scratch every time.
Ignoring categories — you waste time scrolling through all 42.
Dropping a prompt after the first answer without tuning its format and tone for yourself.

exercises.question: Open the library, find a template for your recurring task. Fill in the placeholders. Run it.
exercises.hint: If a template is in the 'Getting started' category — start there. Basic forms work everywhere.

s1.title: Open the ready-made prompt library
s1.why: Ready-made prompts solve 80% of typical tasks. Knowing about them = saving hours.
instructions: In the bottom section of the map — the 'Ready prompts' section.
If it's collapsed — click ▲ to expand.
Browse the list of 10 templates.
s1.validate: You see 10 cards: Create Project, Create Artifact, Expert Audit, etc.
s1.tip: These 10 prompts cover the most frequent tasks. Don't write them from scratch every time.

s2.title: Choose a prompt for YOUR task
s2.why: Blindly copying — little use. Choosing for the task is already half the success.
instructions: Read your current task.
Match it against the prompt list: which is closest in meaning.
Click 'Show' on the right card — read the full template.
s2.example:
My task: 'Prepare a ticket in Linear for adding a filter to the catalog'.
Matching prompt: 'Prepare a task for the developer'.
s2.validate: One prompt chosen that clearly fits the task.
s2.tip: If none fits — that's a signal to create YOUR OWN prompt template in the library.

s3.title: Copy and plug in your context
s3.why: Copying 'as-is' — generic result. Filling in specifics — that's the skill.
instructions: Click 'Copy' — the text goes to the clipboard.
Paste into Claude.
Substitute your values for the placeholders [...].
Send.
s3.example:
BEFORE (placeholders):
Idea: [short description]
Business context: [why this is needed]

AFTER (your task):
Idea: add a brand filter to the product catalog
Business context: users get lost on a page with 500 products; add-to-cart conversion dropped 8% last month
s3.validate: Prompt sent; Claude's answer is specific and tied to your case.
s3.tip: Don't leave placeholders [...] in the final prompt. That's the most common mistake — and Claude answers generically.

s4.title: Fine-tune the prompt for yourself
s4.why: A ready template gives an average answer for everyone. Tuning it to your format, tone and requirements turns it into an answer made just for you.
instructions: Assess the first answer: what's off — format, length, tone, depth?
Add explicit requirements to the prompt: 'answer as a table', 'keep it short, 5 bullets', 'business tone, no fluff'.
Change one parameter at a time and re-run — that way you see what actually worked.
Stop iterating once the answer reliably satisfies you.
s4.example:
Added to the audit template:
'Response format: a 3-column table — Problem | Impact | What to do. No more than 7 rows. Tone — business, no intros.'
→ The answer became predictable and immediately usable for pasting into a ticket.
s4.validate: You have a version of the prompt that reliably produces an answer in the format and tone you need.
s4.tip: The most valuable additions are about output format and length limits. They save the most time on editing the answer.

s5.title: Save the improved version to your library
s5.why: The prompts you adapted are your main asset. Don't lose them.
instructions: Open your library (Notion / Obsidian / text file).
Save the adapted prompt with the tag 'adapted: <your context>'.
Bookmark the template in Cmd+K so it's at hand.
After a week — review: what works, what doesn't.
s5.example:
# Prompt library

## /dev-task — for my project
[adapted prompt]

Notes:
- Works well for feature tickets
- For bug tickets need to add a repro steps section
s5.validate: You have a personal prompt library with at least one adapted template, and it's bookmarked.
s5.tip: In 6 months your library = your main productivity asset. Don't underestimate it.

s6.title: Reuse and share with the team
s6.why: One saved prompt saves minutes. A prompt the whole team uses saves hours and aligns quality without discussion.
instructions: On the next similar task — open the prompt from bookmarks instead of searching again.
Replace only the context for the new case — the structure is already proven.
Share working templates with colleagues (a shared base / channel).
Once a month clean up the library: delete the outdated, promote the best to the top.
s6.example:
The team keeps a shared 'Department prompts' file:
- /dev-task — framing tasks for developers
- /audit — expert feature audit
A new hire takes the ready template and immediately delivers answers of the same quality as the seniors.
s6.validate: You reused a saved prompt at least once and shared at least one template with a colleague or the team.
s6.tip: A prompt reused 10 times pays off many times over. Share it — and team quality will rise on its own.

intro.title: Your first Claude session
intro.subtitle: Open, ask, understand — the basics in one go
intro.whatItIs: The very first tutorial — before models, context, and prompts. What Claude is, how it differs from other AI tools, what to expect and what mistaken expectations to avoid. Suited for someone who has never heard of Claude before.
intro.approach: Don't try to write a complex prompt right away. Make 3 different requests (a question, a task, something creative) and see how Claude responds. Getting acquainted is about calibrating expectations, not achieving a result.
outcomes: Understand that Claude is a conversational AI model, not a search engine
Know who Anthropic is and why they built Constitutional AI
Distinguish Claude's strengths from its typical failures
Have realistic expectations from the first conversation

applyIn.title: First encounter
applyIn.description: Opened [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]], typed 'hi' — now you know what to do next and what NOT to expect.

applyIn.title: Making a decision
applyIn.description: Whether to try Claude for your work at all — after this tutorial you have criteria.

applyIn.title: Explaining to colleagues
applyIn.description: You can tell someone what Claude is in 5 minutes, without fluff.

pitfalls: Expecting Claude to know 'everything' — it has a knowledge cutoff.
Treating the answer as fact — models sometimes confidently get things wrong.
Comparing to Google Search — these are different tools with different strengths.

exercises.question: Ask Claude in one sentence: 'What can you do and where are your limitations?'. Compare the answer to your expectations.
exercises.hint: A good answer — short and honest, no marketing. If you get 'I can do everything' — ask for specifics.

exercises.question: Ask 3 requests: a factual question, a creative task, a breakdown of a simple document. Compare the quality.
exercises.hint: You'll notice — Claude is strong at analysis and phrasing, weaker on fresh facts (without [[node:cap-search|web search]]).

s1.title: Open claude.ai in the browser
s1.why: The very first entry point. Without an account you can't try anything.
instructions: Go to claude.ai.
Register via email or OAuth.
Close the onboarding pop-ups — we'll learn structurally.
s1.validate: You see an empty message field and a greeting from Claude.

s2.title: Ask the first 'factual' question
s2.why: This shows Claude's strong side — structured explanations.
instructions: Write: 'Explain in one paragraph what the HTTP protocol is and what it's for'.
Read the answer.
Notice: Claude answers structurally, without 'lyrical' preambles.
s2.prompt: Explain in one paragraph what the HTTP protocol is and what it's for. No unnecessary details.
s2.validate: You got a short, concrete answer — without a long opener.
s2.tip: Claude is great at explanations. Use it as an 'on-demand teacher' on any topic.

s3.title: Ask about 'today'
s3.why: Now you'll see the limitation — the knowledge cutoff.
instructions: Write: 'What are the tech news from the past week?'.
Notice: Claude will say 'I don't know' or 'My knowledge cutoff is date X'.
This is fine — it's not a bug, it's a known property of the model.
s3.prompt: What are the tech news from the past week?
s3.validate: Claude explicitly mentions the cutoff or warns about outdated information.
s3.tip: For 'fresh' info you need [[node:cap-search|web search]] (see the 'Capabilities' section).

s4.title: Upload a file and discuss it
s4.why: Now you'll see the power of context — Claude works with your data, not just training data.
instructions: Drag a PDF or Word document into the chat (brand guide, article, report).
Write: 'Make a summary in 5 points'.
Read the answer. Notice — Claude cites specific parts of the document.
s4.prompt: Make a summary of this document in 5 points by priority.
s4.validate: The answer is tied to the specific content, not generic.

s5.title: Compare with search
s5.why: To calibrate expectations: where is Claude stronger, where is search.
instructions: Write down two cases from your work.
Think: which is better solved with Google, which with Claude.
Rule: Google — for facts and links. Claude — for analysis, synthesis, phrasing.
s5.validate: You have a clear mental split: when you'll go to Google, when to Claude.

s6.title: Pick your next learning step
s6.why: The intro is over — what matters is not stopping, but immediately mapping out where to grow next.
instructions: Pick one real task from your week where Claude could help.
Decide where to continue: get to grips with [[node:cap-search|web search]] if you need fresh information, or take any next Atlas tutorial.
Write down 1 concrete first step and do it today — while the interest is still warm.
s6.prompt: Here's a real task from my work: {{task}}. Tell me where to start and which 3 first steps to take to solve it with your help.
s6.validate: You have one chosen task and a clear next step — exactly what to learn or do next.
s6.tip: The best learning happens on your own real task, not on abstract examples.

Keeping Claude close all the time, dragging in files, wanting a quick hotkey launch → the Desktop app.
Working with code and project files right in the terminal → Claude Code.

Team gives shared Projects: one [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]], one Knowledge base.
Calculate: 3+ people × $20 (Pro) = $60+. Team costs about the same, but shared.

If N > 15 → upgrade to Pro now.

prompting-techniques.title: Prompting techniques: hands-on
prompting-techniques.subtitle: Few-shot, CoT, XML, Prefill, Structured output — on one task
prompting-techniques.whatItIs: A workshop on 5 fundamental techniques that turn an 'average' prompt into a reliable tool. You apply each technique to the same task to see what each one affects.
prompting-techniques.approach: One baseline prompt → 5 versions with different techniques → comparison. Without comparison you won't feel the effect; with it — the techniques settle into muscle memory.
outcomes: Apply Few-shot, CoT, XML, Prefill consciously — to a specific problem
Get JSON output that parses on the first try
Know which technique helps with which prompt failure
Can iteratively improve a prompt in 3–5 targeted steps

applyIn.title: Exact format
applyIn.description: If you need JSON/table/markdown — Prefill + Structured output technique.

applyIn.title: Complex reasoning
applyIn.description: Analytics, cause-and-effect chains — Chain of Thought.

applyIn.title: Subtle style / tone
applyIn.description: Brand voice, a specific report format — Few-shot examples.

pitfalls: Applying all 5 techniques at once — you won't know what helped. Use one at a time.
Giving contradictory few-shot examples — the model will pick a random pattern.
Prefilling a long starting text — the model stretches to reach it and loses quality. 1–3 anchor tokens is enough.
Asking for 'JSON' without a schema and example — Claude will invent the fields.

exercises.question: Take your baseline prompt and make 5 versions: +CoT, +Few-shot, +XML, +Prefill, +Structured. Compare results.
exercises.hint: Works best on a medium-difficulty task — a simple one will be solved by one technique; a very complex one won't be saved by five.

exercises.question: Find a task in your work routine where you currently manually parse Claude's answer. Rewrite the prompt using Structured output.
exercises.hint: Compare time 'prompt + manual parse' vs 'prompt + auto-parse'. Should be 5–10× savings.

exercises.question: Take a prompt that gives ~70% results. Make 3 iterations using 'one fix → check → next fix'.
exercises.hint: After each iteration write down: what improved, what broke.

s1.title: Lock in a baseline prompt
s1.why: Without a baseline you won't see what each technique improved.
instructions: Take a real task from your work (document audit / data analysis / text structuring).
Phrase the prompt in ONE line — the way you'd normally write in a chat. Example: 'Analyze this text and give conclusions.'
Run in Sonnet, save the result as the baseline.
s1.validate: You have a one-liner prompt + Claude's answer as the baseline.
s1.tip: The more 'average' the baseline quality — the more noticeable the technique's effect. A great baseline is already good; a terrible one — techniques won't save it.

s2.title: Apply Chain of Thought
s2.why: CoT (Chain-of-Thought — asking AI to "think out loud" step by step) gives +20–40% accuracy on tasks where you need to 'derive', not 'recall'.
instructions: Add to the baseline: 'Think step by step. First list the facts, then hypotheses, then conclusions.'
Run in a new chat on the same task. Example prompt: 'Analyze this text. Think step by step: 1) list the facts 2) formulate 2–3 hypotheses 3) check each one 4) give a recommendation.'
Compare the reasoning depth with the baseline.
s2.validate: The answer contains explicit reasoning stages, not just the conclusion.
s2.tip: CoT is not needed for simple questions — just a longer answer. Use it where there's 'logic', not 'fact'.

s3.title: Add Few-shot examples
s3.why: Few-shot (a handful of examples in the prompt that AI mimics) is the most powerful technique for non-standard formats and tone.
instructions: Come up with 2 mini-examples: what input → what output you want.

Structure: 'Example 1: input: ... output: ... Example 2: ... Now do for: ...'. Example prompt: 'Example 1: input: <short text> → output: <in your format>. Example 2: input: <another text> → output: <in your format>. Now do for: <your real input>.'
Run. Check — did the model reproduce the style of the examples?

If the model copies the example verbatim — the examples are too close to your input: make them on-topic but not same-content. If it ignores the example format — add explicitly: 'Format — strictly as in the examples'.
s3.validate: Output follows the pattern of the examples, not its 'own'.
s3.tip: 2–3 examples are usually better than 5+ — more noise, not signal. Use varied examples.

s4.title: Structure with XML tags
s4.why: XML gives +2–3× stability on long prompts with different data types.
instructions: Split the prompt into blocks: <context>, <task>, <examples>, <constraints>.

Put each piece in its own tag. Text inside — plain. Example: '<context>...</context> <task>Analyze the text from <input></task> <input>...</input> <constraints>English only. No introductory phrases. Maximum 5 points.</constraints>'
Run. Notice — the model 'confuses' data and instructions less.
s4.validate: The prompt reads as a structure, not a 'wall of text'. The model clearly separates data from instructions.
s4.tip: XML is for long prompts with different blocks. On a short request — overkill.

s5.title: Lock in format via Prefill and get JSON (Structured output)
s5.why: Prefill firmly sets the start of the answer — the model doesn't 'drift' from the format; together with Structured output it turns the answer into parseable JSON.
instructions: Prefill: in the chat write 'Start the answer exactly with <YOUR_ANCHOR>'. Anchor = the first character of the needed format: { for JSON, | for a table, # for a markdown heading. Example: '<your request>. Start the answer exactly with | (this is a markdown table). No preamble.' In the API, prefill goes as a role: 'assistant' message at the end of messages — the model continues from it.
Structured output: describe the JSON schema explicitly (which fields, types, enum values), give a mini-example of valid output, and close with a Prefill on `{`.

Example prompt: 'Return JSON with schema: {"summary": string (≤200), "topics": [{"name": string, "weight": "low"|"med"|"high"}], "actions": string[]} Example: {"summary": "...", "topics": [{"name": "X", "weight": "high"}], "actions": ["..."]} Data: <your input>. Start the answer exactly with {. No markdown wrapper.'
Run through JSON.parse() — should work on the first try. If the model adds ```json — prefill didn't work, strengthen: 'WITHOUT markdown wrapper. Raw JSON only'.
If fields are sometimes missing — add 'all fields are required' to the schema. If fields contain extra noise — show a bad and good example: 'don't do this: ...; do this: ...'.
s5.validate: The answer starts with your anchor, without 'Sure, here is...' openers; JSON parses on the first try, fields match the schema.
s5.tip: Prefill 1–3 anchor tokens — no more. Don't rely on 'the model will figure it out': write the schema and required fields explicitly.

s6.title: Iteration: one failure — one fix
s6.why: A method for improving a prompt without rewriting from scratch.
instructions: Take a prompt that gives ~70%.
Find ONE specific failure (e.g., 'the output is too generic').
Make ONE change (role / constraint / example).
Run on 2–3 different inputs. Record: helped / didn't.
Repeat 2–3 times.
s6.validate: You have v4 vs v1 of the prompt — a noticeable difference without a full rewrite.
s6.tip: Change 5 things at once — you won't know what helped. One step = one hypothesis.

welcome.title: Getting to know Claude
welcome.subtitle: What Claude is, what modes it has, and how to set it up for yourself
welcome.whatItIs: The very first lesson. Explains what Claude is, how it differs from other assistants, what its working modes are (Chat, Cowork, Code), and how to make it useful for your own tasks.
welcome.approach: Every step has buttons that open the right place for you. You do not need to hunt for things in the menus. Read, click, try.
outcomes: You know what Claude is and who built it
You understand how Haiku, Sonnet and Opus models differ
You can tell Chat, Cowork and Code apart
You picked the version you need: the website, the app, or Code
You know how to tune Claude with Custom Instructions and Projects

applyIn.title: Light tasks
applyIn.description: A letter, a translation, an explanation, a short summary. Chat at claude.ai is enough.

applyIn.title: Long work on one task
applyIn.description: Going through documents, multi-step tasks. Cowork in the desktop app fits.

applyIn.title: Code and files
applyIn.description: Programming, automation. Claude Code in the terminal is what you want.

pitfalls: Sticking to one mode only. Each one has its strengths. Different tools for different jobs.
Not setting Claude up for yourself. Without Custom Instructions it answers generically, with no idea about your context.
Ignoring model trade-offs. Haiku is fast but less accurate. Opus is smart but slow and pricey.

exercises.question: Open claude.ai and ask Claude to list three points that make it different from ChatGPT.
exercises.hint: Compare the answer with what you read in this lesson. It shows you how Claude thinks about itself.

s1.title: What Claude is
s1.why: To know who you are about to use.
instructions: Claude is a family of smart assistants that reply to you in text. They are built by a company called Anthropic, founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers.
Inside Claude there are three models of different power. Haiku is the fast and cheap one. Sonnet is the middle ground and the default. Opus is the smartest, for hard tasks.
You usually do not pick the model by hand. Claude picks the right one for the task. You can switch in settings when you need to.
Claude looks similar to ChatGPT in spirit, but differs in details. It has longer memory inside one chat, is more careful with facts, and stays calmer on touchy topics.
s1.validate: You understand that Claude is built by Anthropic and comes in three models (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus).
s1.tip: Sonnet covers about 95 percent of tasks. Switch to Opus only when you need deeper reasoning.

s2.title: Three ways to work with Claude
s2.why: Understand the difference between modes so you can pick yours.
instructions: Chat. A regular conversation in your browser or app. Ask a question, get an answer. Best for short tasks: letters, translations, explanations, idea brainstorming.

Cowork. A mode in the desktop app where Claude can work with your files, documents and even your screen, step by step. Best for long tasks: working through documents, writing long texts, doing analysis.
Code. A separate tool for programmers. It runs in the terminal on your computer. It can read and change code files, run commands. You only need it if you write code.
Next, we will walk through the modes: we start with the simplest one, Chat, then cover Cowork and Code together. If you are not a programmer, the Code part is safe to skip.
s2.validate: You remember the three names and what they are for: Chat for short tasks, Cowork for long ones, Code for programmers.
s2.tip: Most people only need Chat. Cowork and Code are for those who want to go deeper.

s3.title: Chat. The easiest way to start
s3.why: This is the basic mode everyone starts with. Nothing to install.
instructions: Press the button below to open claude.ai in a new tab.
Sign in by email or through Google. Sign-up is free. You do not need a paid plan to begin.
After signing in you will see an input field. That is Chat.
Copy the question below and paste it into the field. Press send and read the answer.
s3.prompt: In three simple sentences, tell me how you are different from ChatGPT and what you do best.
s3.validate: You got a reply from Claude in Chat on [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]].
s3.tip: If the answer is too long, write: shorter, one sentence. Claude will get it.

s4.title: Cowork and Code. When the task is bigger than one question
s4.why: Cowork is for working on one topic for a while (a long text, going through a document, a report). Code is Claude's most powerful mode for people who work with code. If you are not a programmer, you can just read about Code.
instructions: Cowork lives in a separate app for Mac or Windows. Download it from Claude's website with the button below.

In Cowork you can give Claude files (documents, spreadsheets, images) or grant it screen access. It then works with them on its own, step by step. Examples: go through these 50 pages and surface the key risks; read my email and draft replies; help me write a long article from this outline.
Cowork is not for every task. If you only have a quick question, stay in Chat. Serious Cowork work needs a Pro subscription, but you can try it for free in a limited way.

Claude Code is a tool for developers that runs in your terminal (the dark window with a command line on your computer). It can read and edit code files directly on your disk, run commands, find bugs, refactor, explain unfamiliar code.

Installing Code is one terminal command. It needs Node.js, a free program that runs commands. There is a dedicated tutorial that walks through it. Code does not replace Chat or Cowork, it adds to them. If you are not a programmer, you can skip Code entirely, and that is fine.
s4.validate: You understand that Cowork is the desktop app for long tasks involving files, and Code is a terminal tool for people who work with code.
s4.tip: Not sure whether you need Cowork or Code? Start with Chat. You can always come back to the advanced modes.

actions.label: Install Claude Code step by step

s5.title: Tuning. Make Claude yours
s5.why: By default Claude answers in a generic way. [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]] help it understand your context, and Projects are handy when you have a series of similar tasks.
instructions: Custom Instructions is a short message Claude sees inside every conversation of yours. You write your role, your industry, the tone you want, and what NOT to do. Example: I am an accountant in a small business. Answer briefly, without fluff, in simple words. Do not give legal advice.

Where to find it on the website: in claude.ai open your profile (top right), then Settings → Custom Instructions. The desktop app has a similar setting. Set it once and it always works. Update it when something starts to annoy you in the replies.

A Project is a folder where you keep several chats on one topic. All chats inside a Project share knowledge and instructions. Example: a Project called Marketing for company X, with 20 chats all sharing the same uploaded files: the brand guide, past reports, the yearly plan.
Where to find Projects: on claude.ai look in the left menu for Projects, then New Project. Serious use needs a Pro plan. Do not make a Project for a single task, use it for things that repeat.
s5.validate: You understand that Custom Instructions is your profile card for Claude, and a Project is a workspace for a series of related tasks.
s5.tip: Do not write a wall of text in Custom Instructions. Five to ten lines about you and how you want to talk is more than enough.

s6.title: What to do right now
s6.why: Knowledge fades without action. Make at least one move.
instructions: If you are just meeting Claude for the first time, open claude.ai and ask your first question in Chat.
If you already like Claude and want to use it regularly, set up Custom Instructions. The quality jump is large.
If you need long work with files and documents, download the Claude app with Cowork support.
If you are a programmer and want the advanced mode, take the tutorial that installs Claude Code.
s6.validate: You picked what to try next and made at least one click in that direction.
s6.tip: Do not try to master everything in a day. Come back to the map when questions show up in your real work.

outputs: Clear sense of modes: Chat / Cowork / Code
Realistic expectations from Claude

claude-cowork.title: Your first task with Claude Cowork
claude-cowork.subtitle: From open to result — autonomous workflow
claude-cowork.whatItIs: A hands-on walkthrough of Claude Cowork: open the Desktop app, connect a folder, describe a task as an outcome, let Claude run it, and review the results. You will complete a real file task from start to finish.
claude-cowork.approach: Describe WHAT you want, not HOW to do it. Claude figures out the steps. Start with a small, low-risk task on a test folder — not your critical files. Keep the Desktop app open the entire time.

outcomes.0: Opened Cowork and understand the interface
outcomes.1: Connected a specific folder (not your whole drive)
outcomes.3: Reviewed Claude's plan before approving it
outcomes.4: Checked the finished output and know how to iterate
outcomes.5: Put a proven task on a Scheduled cadence

0.title: File organization
0.description: Sort downloads, rename files by date, group by project — set it up once, run it weekly.

1.title: Document processing
1.description: Extract data from PDFs, summarize meeting notes, convert formats across a folder of files.

2.title: Scheduled automation
2.description: After mastering a task manually, use /schedule to run it automatically on a cadence.

pitfalls.0: Closing the Desktop app mid-task — Cowork stops immediately.
pitfalls.1: Describing HOW to do the task step-by-step — describe the outcome instead.
pitfalls.2: Connecting your entire drive — connect only the specific folder you need.
pitfalls.3: Using Cowork for simple questions — it consumes significantly more usage quota than regular chat.

exercises.question: Run a second Cowork task: ask Claude to create a summary report of all .txt files in your test folder. Review the output and try one correction via natural language.
exercises.hint: Say what is wrong with the result, not how to fix it. Claude will figure out the correction.

exercises.question: Put your file-organization task on a Scheduled cadence (for example, every Monday morning) and on the next run confirm the result arrived without you doing anything.
exercises.hint: The task must run manually at least once first — Scheduled repeats a proven result, it does not debug a new one.

s1.title: Open Cowork in Claude Desktop
s1.why: Cowork only exists in the Desktop app (Mac/Windows). The web version does not have it. You need a Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plan.

instructions.0: Download and install Claude Desktop from claude.ai/download if you haven't already.
instructions.1: Sign in with your Claude account (Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise required).
instructions.2: In the Claude Desktop window, look for the 'Cowork' tab or button — it is separate from the regular chat.
instructions.3: Click it to open the Cowork interface. You will see a task input area and a section for connected folders.

s1.validate: You see the Cowork task interface — different from the regular chat.
s1.tip: Keep the Desktop app open during the entire tutorial. Cowork tasks stop the moment you close the app.

s2.title: Connect a folder
s2.why: Claude needs explicit permission to read and write files. You choose exactly which folder to expose — Claude cannot access anything outside it.

instructions.0: In the Cowork interface, find the 'Connect folder' or 'Add folder' option.
instructions.1: Choose a specific working folder — for example, a 'Cowork-test' folder on your Desktop.
instructions.2: Do NOT connect your entire Documents or Desktop root — start small and specific.
instructions.3: Confirm the connection. The folder should now appear as available in the Cowork context.

s2.validate: Your chosen folder appears as connected. Claude now has read/write access to it.
s2.tip: For your first task, create a test folder with a few non-critical files. This lets you experiment safely.

troubleshoot.Cannot find 'Connect folder' button: Check that you are in the Cowork tab, not the regular chat. The interface is different.
troubleshoot.Permission denied by OS: On macOS, go to System Settings → Privacy & Security → Files & Folders and grant Claude Desktop access.

s3.title: Describe your task as an outcome
s3.why: The key difference from regular chat: describe WHAT you want as a finished result, not the steps to get there. Claude plans the steps itself.

instructions.0: In the Cowork task field, type your task as an outcome.
instructions.1: Be specific: mention the folder, the type of files, and the desired end state.
instructions.2: Include the output format if it matters (e.g. 'create a summary as a .txt file').
instructions.3: Submit the task. Claude will show you a plan BEFORE starting.

s3.example:
Good: 'In the Cowork-test folder, group all files by extension into subfolders (e.g. /images, /docs, /other), then create a file called index.txt that lists what was moved and where.'

Bad: 'First check the folder, then create subfolders, then move each file...' — don't prescribe steps.
s3.validate: Claude presents a plan showing what it will do. Read it before approving.
s3.tip: If the plan looks wrong, type a correction before approving. It is faster to fix the plan than fix the output.

s4.title: Approve and monitor
s4.why: Cowork runs autonomously once approved. You can watch its progress or step away — both are valid. The key is keeping the Desktop app open.

instructions.0: Review Claude's plan carefully — check that it describes what you actually want.
instructions.1: Click Approve (or equivalent) to start the task.
instructions.2: Watch the progress indicator. Claude shows what it is doing at each step.
instructions.3: You can step away — Claude will continue. Come back when it signals completion.
instructions.4: Do not close the Desktop app. If you need to lock your screen, that is fine — just do not quit the application.

s4.validate: Task reaches 100% and Claude shows a summary of what was done.

troubleshoot.Task stopped unexpectedly: Most likely the Desktop app was closed or lost internet. Reopen it and check if the task can be resumed.
troubleshoot.Claude asks for permission mid-task: Some actions (like deletion) require your explicit approval. Read the request and approve or deny.

s5.title: Review the output and iterate
s5.why: Diligence: the first result is a strong draft, not necessarily final. Open the folder, check the files, and correct anything that missed the mark — in natural language.

instructions.0: Open the connected folder in your file manager and check the output.
instructions.1: Compare what Claude did against your original description.
instructions.2: If something is wrong, describe the issue in plain language in the Cowork task field.
instructions.3: For recurring tasks you are satisfied with, type /schedule to set up automatic runs.

s5.validate: Output matches your intent. You know how to describe corrections.
s5.tip: Say what is wrong ('the images folder is missing PDF files that have images embedded'), not how to fix it. Claude will figure out the correction.

s6.title: Put the task on a Scheduled cadence
s6.why: Once a task is proven and the result satisfies you, there is no point running it by hand every time. A Scheduled cadence repeats the already-verified task automatically — for example, every Monday morning — without you lifting a finger.

instructions.0: Make sure the task has already run manually at least once and the result is correct.
instructions.1: In the Cowork task field, type /schedule (or open the Scheduled menu).
instructions.2: Set the cadence in plain words: 'every Monday at 9 AM' or 'once a day'.
instructions.3: Save the schedule and confirm the task appears in the Scheduled list with its next run time.
instructions.4: Remember: the Desktop app must be open at the scheduled run time — otherwise the task will not start.

s6.validate: The task appears in the Scheduled list with a next run time and repeats without your involvement.
s6.tip: Only schedule proven, low-risk tasks. An automatic run repeats the result literally — it will not stop to ask if something in the folder has changed.

claude-cowork.trigger: A task involves a folder of files and copy-pasting into the browser is painful.
inputs: Task described as the expected outcome
outputs: Connected working folder
A real file task completed end-to-end
Clear sense of Chat vs Cowork
