s2.tip: An output example works more strongly than a verbal description: Claude copies the example's shape more precisely than it interprets abstract rules.

s3.title: JSON vs table vs CSV — what when
s3.why: The format is chosen for the recipient and the shape of the data. The wrong choice complicates parsing: nested JSON where CSV would suffice, or a table where nested objects are needed.
instructions: JSON — when the data is nested (objects inside arrays) and goes to an API or code
CSV — when the data is flat, uniform rows, and an import into a table/Excel is needed
Markdown table — when a human reads the answer in chat or it is pasted into a document
XML — when the target system requires it or you need explicit block boundaries; see [[node:pr-xml|XML tags]]
For CSV and tables fix the order and names of columns, for JSON — the exact object shape
s3.validate: You can justify the format choice based on the recipient (human/code) and the data shape (flat/nested).
s3.tip: Flat tabular data is almost always simpler and more reliable in CSV or a table than in JSON — less syntax for the model to break.

s4.title: A worked example with a schema description
s4.why: Separate rules work more weakly than one assembled prompt where the schema, types, and example go together. A full example shows Claude the exact goal and sharply reduces answer variance.
instructions: Assemble in one prompt: the task, the list of fields with types, the constraints, and the output example
For example: return JSON {"summary": string (≤200 chars), "risks": [{"id": string, "severity": "low"|"med"|"high"}]}
Show one fully filled-in example of this JSON with values
Add the output instruction: "no preamble, start with {"
Check that the example itself is valid — the model will copy its shape, including mistakes
s4.validate: The prompt contains the task, the schema with types, a filled-in example, and the output format instruction — all in one place.
s4.tip: Before sending, run your reference example through a parser yourself: if it doesn't parse for you, the model's answer won't parse either.

s5.title: Reliability: prefill, validation, extra text
s5.why: Even with a good schema the model adds a ```json wrapper or a phrase like "Sure, here is the answer". Prefill removes the preamble, and validation catches deviations before they reach the system. More on the technique — [[node:pr-prefill|prefill]].
instructions: Use prefill: put the opening character ({ or [) as the start of the model's answer
In the instruction explicitly forbid preamble and a markdown wrapper
After receiving the answer, validate it in code (JSON.parse, schema check)
If extra text arrives — cut to the first { and after the last }, or tighten the prefill
On repeated failures add a counter-example: "don't wrap in ```, don't write an intro"
s5.validate: The answer starts straight with the structure, without a wrapper or preamble, and passes the parser/validator successfully.
s5.tip: Prefill is the cheapest way to remove chatter: the model physically continues from the inserted brace and cannot start with an intro phrase.

s6.title: Mistakes and checking
s6.why: Structured output seems ready until you hit an edge case: empty data, a non-standard value, long text. A final check catches this before production.
instructions: Run the prompt on 5–10 different inputs, including empty and anomalous ones
Check that types and enums are respected always, not only on convenient examples
Make sure missing data is handled as you defined (null/omit)
Check boundary constraints: string length, a number out of range
Record the failed cases and refine the schema or prefill for them
s6.validate: On a set of varied and edge inputs the answers stably pass the validator without manual fixing.
s6.tip: Deliberately feed a "bad" input (empty, very long, missing the needed data) — that's exactly where the holes in the schema surface, invisible on perfect examples.

prompt-iterate.title: Prompt iteration
prompt-iterate.subtitle: Run → find one failure → one edit → repeat
prompt-iterate.whatItIs:
A systematic way to get a prompt to the result without rewriting it from scratch. Instead of "I'll redo it all", you treat the prompt as a hypothesis: you run it, find ONE concrete failure, make ONE edit (role / example / constraint), compare — and repeat the cycle.

Most "bad" prompts turn into "great" ones after 3-5 targeted iterations. This course gives you the method: how to lock in a baseline, how to find a real failure, how to change one thing at a time and know exactly what helped. It builds on [[node:prompting|basic prompting]] and works together with [[node:pr-fewshot|few-shot examples]].
prompt-iterate.approach: The key rule: one edit per iteration. If you change five things at once, it's impossible to tell what worked. Don't rewrite the working parts: fix a specific failure, not a "general feeling". And always compare with the previous version on the same inputs.
outcomes: You understand when iteration beats rewriting from scratch
You can lock in a baseline and define a criterion for "good"
You find ONE concrete failure instead of a vague "I don't like it"
You make one edit at a time and see its effect
You know when to stop and save the prompt as a template

applyIn.title: A working prompt that's "almost there"
applyIn.description: The prompt gives ~70% of the result. Instead of rewriting, you finish it off in 2-3 iterations.

applyIn.title: A prompt for the team
applyIn.description: You bring the prompt to stable quality and save it as a template, so the whole team gets the same result.

applyIn.title: Automation and recurring tasks
applyIn.description: A prompt that runs every day is worth polishing once with iterations — the savings compound.

pitfalls: Changing several things in one iteration — afterwards it's unclear what actually helped
No criterion for "good" — iterations run on gut feeling and never end
Rewriting the whole prompt and losing the working parts
Testing on a single input — an edit "fixes" one case and breaks the rest
Not stopping in time: polishing something that's already good enough

exercises.question: Take a prompt you're "almost happy" with. Run it on 3 different inputs and write down one concrete failure for each. Which failure is common across them?
exercises.hint: Look for a pattern, not a one-off glitch. A failure common to all 3 inputs is the best candidate for the first edit.

exercises.question: Define a criterion for "good" for your prompt in one verifiable sentence (not "high quality", but "answer ≤ 5 bullets, each with an example").
exercises.hint: If the criterion can't be checked yes/no, it's too vague — reformulate it.

exercises.question: Make ONE edit (add a role OR one example OR one constraint) and compare the new answer with the old one on the same inputs. Did it get better against your criterion?
exercises.hint: If it got worse, roll the edit back — that's a normal part of the cycle. The hypothesis wasn't confirmed.

s1.title: Why systematic iteration, not rewriting from scratch
s1.why: Rewriting a prompt from scratch throws away the working parts and starts over every time. Iteration keeps what already works and fixes only the problem — it's many times faster and clearer.
instructions: Adopt the mindset: a prompt is a hypothesis, not a final text. You improve it in cycles, not in one heroic rewrite.
Memorize the four-step cycle: run → find one failure → one edit → compare.
Don't throw away the old version: working parts (format, good phrasing) should be preserved, not lost in a rewrite.
Set the course goal: learn to change ONE thing at a time and know exactly what helped.
s1.validate: You can explain in your own words why "3-5 targeted edits" is usually better than "rewrite everything from scratch".
s1.tip: If you feel like rewriting everything, that's a sign you haven't found a concrete failure yet. Find the failure first.

s2.title: Lock in a baseline and a criterion for "good"
s2.why: Without a starting point and a success criterion, you can't tell whether an edit helped. Iteration without a criterion turns into endless polishing on gut feeling.
instructions: Save the current version of the prompt as the baseline (version 0) — this is what you'll compare against.
Run the baseline on 3 fixed inputs and save all three answers — this is your reference for comparison.
Define a criterion for "good" in one verifiable sentence: what specifically must be in the answer (format, length, tone, presence of examples).
Check the criterion as yes/no: can you say unambiguously from the answer whether it's met? If not, reformulate it.
s2.validate: You have a saved baseline, three reference answers, and one verifiable criterion for "good".
s2.tip: Use the same 3 inputs throughout the course — otherwise comparing versions loses its meaning.

s3.title: Find ONE concrete failure
s3.why: "I don't like the result" isn't a failure, it's a feeling. An edit can only target a concrete problem. One clear failure = one clear hypothesis for an edit.
instructions: Compare the three reference answers against your criterion for "good" and write down what exactly is wrong in each.
Find a common pattern: which failure repeats across several inputs — it matters more than a one-off glitch.
State the failure concretely: not "too long", but "the answer is a solid paragraph instead of a list of ≤5 bullets".
Pick ONE failure for this iteration — the most frequent or most painful. Note the rest for later.
s3.validate: You have one concrete, verifiable failure stated as "it should be X, but it comes out as Y".
s3.tip: If there are many failures, start with the one that breaks the most answers. Fix them one at a time.

s4.title: Make ONE edit and compare
s4.why: One edit per iteration is the only way to know exactly what worked. If you change several things at once, the result may improve, but you won't know why and you won't be able to reproduce it.
instructions: Pick ONE type of edit for your failure: clarify the role, add one [[node:pr-fewshot|few-shot example]], or add one constraint.
Make only that edit — don't touch anything else in the prompt.
Run the new version on the same 3 inputs as the baseline.
Compare the new answers with the old ones against the criterion for "good": better, worse, or no change?
If it's worse or unchanged, roll the edit back and formulate a different hypothesis. That's a normal part of the cycle.
s4.validate: You made exactly one edit, ran it on the same inputs, and can say whether it helped or not.
s4.tip: Keep a short log: "edit → effect". After 3-4 iterations you'll see which techniques really work for your task.

s5.title: When to stop and save as a template
s5.why: Iteration can go on forever. The criterion for "good" from step 2 is your stop signal. Once the prompt reliably passes the criterion, further polishing spends time without payoff.
instructions: Stop when the prompt passes your criterion for "good" on all 3 inputs — the goal is reached.
Check stability: run the final version on 1-2 new inputs too, to make sure the edits didn't overfit to the three test cases.
Save the final prompt as a template with placeholders for the variable parts — add it to your library of [[node:ready-prompts|ready prompts]].
Write down the criterion for "good" and 1-2 example inputs next to it — so the next time you edit, you know what to compare against.
s5.validate: You have a final prompt template that passes the criterion, and it's saved for reuse.
s5.tip: "Good enough" is usually reachable in 3-5 iterations. If you've gone past 8, the criterion is probably vague — go back to step 2.

s6.title: Common mistakes and a final check
s6.why: Two mistakes kill iteration: changing everything at once (unclear what helped) and working without a criterion (unclear when to stop). The final check catches them before you waste time.
instructions: Mistake "change everything at once": the rule is one edit per iteration. If you changed three things, you don't know which worked.
Mistake "no criterion": without a verifiable "good", iterations never end. The criterion is set in step 2, before any edits.
Mistake "single input": an edit tuned to one example breaks the rest. Test on at least 3 inputs.
Final check: run the checklist — got a baseline? got a verifiable criterion? changed one thing at a time? tested on 3 inputs? saved as a template?
s6.validate: You pass the whole checklist for your prompt: baseline, criterion, one edit at a time, 3 inputs, saved template.
s6.tip: Print the 5-point checklist and keep it nearby — it turns iteration from intuition into a reproducible process.

agent-principles.title: Agent design principles
agent-principles.subtitle: Narrow purpose, a clear trigger, least-tools, and a verifiable output
agent-principles.whatItIs: A course on the six properties that separate a reliable [[node:agents|agent]] from a long prompt: narrow purpose, a single clear trigger, a limited tool set, a verifiable structured output, and explicit boundaries and safety. It's a checklist before launch, not a post-mortem.
agent-principles.approach: We move principle by principle like a filter: at each step you state one property of your future agent and immediately test it against your own example. By the sixth step you have a ready specification you can ship or hand off to a team.
outcomes: State the agent's purpose in one sentence with no "and"
Describe a trigger that makes it clear when the agent fires and when it doesn't
Assemble a minimal tool set for the task (least-tools)
Pin down an output format that can be checked automatically
Describe boundaries: what the agent does NOT do and what needs confirmation

applyIn.title: Before building a subagent
applyIn.description: Run a [[node:cc-subagents|subagent]] idea through the six principles and cut whatever isn't ready before writing the first line.

applyIn.title: Reviewing someone else's agent
applyIn.description: Take an existing agent and check it against the checklist: where the weak spot is, there's the cause of the "weird behavior".

applyIn.title: Handing off to a team
applyIn.description: A principle-based spec is a document another person can use to understand the agent without your verbal explanations.

pitfalls: A purpose with "and": an agent that "reviews PRs and writes tests and deploys" is three agents
A vague trigger: unclear when the agent should fire and when it should stay silent
30 tools "just in case" — the agent picks the wrong ones and behavior drifts
Free-text output that can't be checked automatically
No boundaries: the agent silently performs a dangerous action without confirmation

exercises.question: State the purpose of a spell-checking agent for articles in one sentence with no "and". What stays out of scope?
exercises.hint: If you're tempted to add "and also checks facts" — that's a separate agent. Purpose = one verifiable action.

exercises.question: For a reviewer agent, what is the minimal tool set, and why does it NOT need write access to the repo?
exercises.hint: Review is reading and commenting. Write access widens the risk surface with no benefit to the task.

exercises.question: Design an output format for an email-classifier agent that can be verified automatically.
exercises.hint: Think of a fixed set of labels and a structure like {label, confidence}, not "an answer in its own words".

s1.title: Why design principles matter
s1.why: Most "non-working" agents fail not because of the model but because one of the basic principles was skipped at design time. Principles turn a fuzzy idea into a verifiable specification.
instructions: Write down the agent that "almost works" or that you want to build — in one phrase
Say the six properties out loud: purpose, trigger, tools, output, boundaries, safety
Mark the points you "didn't think about" — that's usually where the agent breaks
Adopt the rule: 2+ skipped points = the agent isn't ready to launch
s1.validate: You have a list of six points and an honest mark of where the gaps are.
s1.tip: Principles are a filter BEFORE launch. It's cheaper to discard a bad idea on paper than to debug it in prod.

s2.title: Narrow purpose and one clear trigger
s2.why: An agent with a broad purpose picks different strategies on similar inputs — behavior becomes unpredictable. A narrow purpose and an explicit trigger make the agent deterministic and understandable.
instructions: State the purpose in one sentence with no "and"
If an "and" appears — split into two agents or choose the main one
Describe the trigger: what event or request fires the agent
Describe the anti-trigger: when the agent must NOT fire
Cross-check the trigger against the purpose — they must point to the same thing
s2.validate: The purpose is one phrase with no "and"; for the trigger it's clear both when it fires and when it stays silent.
s2.tip: A good trigger can be read to an outsider and they'll guess what the agent does. It's like the narrow scope of a [[node:skills|skill]].

s3.title: A limited tool set (least-tools)
s3.why: Every extra tool is an extra behavior path and an extra risk surface. A minimal set makes the agent more reliable and predictable: less choice means fewer mistakes.
instructions: Write down every tool that comes to mind for the task
For each, ask: "can the agent fulfill its purpose without it?" If yes — drop it
Split into read and write: keep write only if it's literally in the purpose
For external data, decide whether an [[node:mcp|MCP]] source is needed or local tools suffice
Keep the minimal set and record a reason for each tool
s3.validate: Every tool in the final list has a written "why" justification.
s3.tip: "Least-tools" is like "least-privilege" in security: grant exactly what one task needs, no more.

s4.title: A verifiable structured output
s4.why: If the agent's output is free text, it can't be checked automatically and can't be reliably passed down the chain. A structured output turns the agent into a dependable building block rather than a paragraph generator.
instructions: Define exactly what the agent should return — data, a label, a list of actions
Pin down the format: the set of fields, allowed values, required keys
Describe at least one auto-check: "the output is valid if field X exists and is from set Y"
Add an explicit format for the "no result" case, not an empty string
Confirm the output can feed the next step with no manual editing
s4.validate: There is a description of the output format and at least one rule by which it can be checked automatically.
s4.tip: Fixed labels beat free text: {label, confidence} is script-checkable, a paragraph is not.

s5.title: Boundaries and safety: what the agent does NOT do
s5.why: Without explicit boundaries an agent will sooner or later take a dangerous action because "it seemed logical". Stated boundaries and confirmation points are insurance against irreversible mistakes.
instructions: Write down the list of forbidden actions: what the agent never does
Mark irreversible actions (deletion, sending, payment) — they need a confirmation request
Describe a fallback: what to do when the task is out of scope or data is missing
Make dangerous actions idempotent or at least visible in the logs
Check that the boundaries don't contradict the purpose from step 2
s5.validate: There is a "the agent does NOT do" list and a confirmation rule for irreversible actions.
s5.tip: The rule is simple: an irreversible action only after an explicit "yes" from a human. This is a baseline safety requirement for any [[node:agents|agent]].

s6.title: A good-agent checklist and the final check
s6.why: The collected principles must be run as a single checklist, otherwise it's easy to miss a gap between steps. The final check is the last filter before launch.
instructions: Walk the checklist: purpose, trigger, tools, output, boundaries, safety
On each point answer "ready / not ready" — no "almost"
If anything is "not ready" — go back to the matching step and finish stating it
Run a mental dry run on one real input: what the agent does step by step
Record the final specification as a document that can be handed off
s6.validate: All six points are marked "ready" and there is one dry run on a real example.
s6.tip: A checklist-based spec reads like a short brief — another person can reproduce the agent from it without your explanations.

agent-code-reviewer.title: Code Reviewer Agent
agent-code-reviewer.subtitle: Auto-review of PRs and commits against a checklist: security, readability, tests, regressions
agent-code-reviewer.whatItIs: A Code Reviewer agent is a specialized [[node:agents|agent]] that reads code changes (diff, PR files) and produces comments against a clear checklist: security, readability, test coverage and regression risk. It doesn't replace the human expert — it lifts the pre-review routine off them: by the time a human looks, the obvious issues are already found and sorted by severity.
agent-code-reviewer.approach: The course builds the agent from boundaries to rollout. First we fix what the agent does and does NOT do, then we write the checklist as the source of truth, set the role and instructions, connect the code context (diff/files), standardize the output format by severity (no style bikeshedding) and embed the agent into the PR process. Every step ends with a check on a real PR.
outcomes: You understand the reviewer agent's boundaries: what it catches and where a human is needed
You have a written review checklist (security, readability, tests, regressions)
The agent is set up with a role and instructions that give reproducible results
Findings come out in a single format by severity, without formatting noise
The agent is embedded in the PR process and genuinely saves expert time

applyIn.title: Team PR process
applyIn.description: The agent passes every PR before a human and leaves comments by severity — the expert sees already-filtered code.

applyIn.title: Solo development
applyIn.description: Before committing you run the diff through the agent as a second pair of eyes: it catches leaked secrets, missing tests, risky edits.

applyIn.title: Onboarding and learning
applyIn.description: A newcomer sees what the agent pays attention to and picks up the team's review standards faster.

pitfalls: Trusting only the agent — it doesn't replace architectural thinking or product context
Keeping the checklist in your head, not on paper — results differ every time and aren't repeatable
Mixing style and substance — the agent drowns in indentation comments while real bugs get lost
Feeding the agent the whole repo instead of the diff — it loses focus and misses the point of the change
Comments without severity — a human can't tell what blocks merge from what's cosmetic

exercises.question: Write three checklist items from the "security" category that the agent must check on every PR.
exercises.hint: Think about what most often leaks into commits: secrets in code, missing input validation, unsafe dependencies.

exercises.question: Why should the agent return findings tagged with severity rather than just a flat list?
exercises.hint: Picture a PR with 12 comments: what does the human do first? Severity separates blockers from nice-to-haves.

exercises.question: Explain where the boundary lies between the reviewer agent and the human expert.
exercises.hint: The agent is great at checkable rules from the checklist. But who decides the architecture is the right choice?

s1.title: Why a reviewer agent and where its boundaries lie
s1.why: Without clear boundaries the agent either pretends to be an expert (dangerous) or gets ignored. First fix the area of responsibility: checkable items go to the agent, architectural decisions and product context stay with the human.
instructions: Write one sentence: the agent checks PRs/commits against a checklist (security, readability, tests, regressions).
List what the agent does NOT do: doesn't settle architecture debates, doesn't judge business logic without context, doesn't block merge on its own.
Capture the principle from [[node:ag-principles|agent principles]]: a narrow role with a clear boundary is more reliable than a "universal reviewer".
Agree with the team (or yourself) that the agent's output is input for a human, not a final verdict.
s1.validate: You have two short notes: "agent does" and "agent does NOT", both fitting in a couple of lines.
s1.tip: If the area of responsibility can't be described in one paragraph, it's too broad — narrow it.

s2.title: Define the review checklist
s2.why: The checklist is the source of truth for the agent. Without it every review is different and unrepeatable. A written list makes results predictable and verifiable.
instructions: Split the checklist into 4 categories: security, readability, tests, regressions.
Security: secrets in code, input validation, unsafe dependencies, access rights.
Readability: clear names, no dead code, reasonable function size.
Tests: are new branches covered, are existing ones broken, are there tests for bug fixes.
Regressions: does the change break a public contract, migrations, backward compatibility.
s2.validate: The checklist is written as a bulleted list under 4 headings and fits on one screen.
s2.tip: Start with 3-4 items per category — expand later from real findings, not preemptively.

s3.title: Set the agent's role and instructions
s3.why: Role and instructions turn the checklist into behavior. A clear wording ("you are a reviewer, check strictly against the checklist") gives reproducible results instead of the model's free improvisation.
instructions: Describe the role: "You are a strict but constructive code reviewer. Check only against the checklist below."
Paste the checklist from step 2 directly into the agent's instructions.
Forbid style/formatting checks — that's the linter's job, not the agent's.
If you use [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]], set this up as a subagent or [[node:skills|skill]] with a "review PR" trigger.
Add a rule: every finding references the checklist item it violates.
s3.validate: The agent's instruction contains the role, the checklist and an explicit ban on style comments.
s3.tip: Ask the agent to briefly justify each finding — this sharply reduces false positives.

s4.title: Connect the code context (diff/files)
s4.why: The agent is only as good as its context. The diff focuses attention on the change; the affected files in full give an understanding of the surroundings. The whole repository is just noise.
instructions: Feed the agent the PR diff as the main input — that's what actually changed.
For each affected file, give enough surrounding code to understand the context of the edit.
Don't load the whole repository: the agent will lose focus and miss the point.
If the edit touches a public API or contract, add the consumer file to assess regressions.
s4.validate: On a test PR the agent sees the diff and the needed surroundings, but not the whole project.
s4.tip: Big PR? Ask the agent to first list the affected areas, then review them one at a time.

s5.title: Output format: findings by severity, no style
s5.why: An unprioritized list is useless: a human can't tell what blocks merge from what's cosmetic. A single format by severity makes the output scannable and actionable.
instructions: Set severity levels: blocker, major, minor (you may add info).
Each finding = severity + file/line + checklist item + what's wrong + a suggestion.
Forbid comments about formatting and personal style preferences.
Ask the agent for a short summary at the end: how many blocker/major/minor were found.
If there are no findings, the agent must explicitly say "no checklist comments" rather than stay silent.
s5.validate: Output on a test PR is a structured list by severity with a summary, no style comments.
s5.tip: A blocker should mean "can't merge". If there are many blockers on every PR, the threshold is set too high.

s6.title: Rollout into the PR process + common mistakes
s6.why: The agent only adds value when embedded in a real process. The goal is that by the time a human reviews, the obvious is already found and sorted, and the expert focuses on architecture.
instructions: Decide the trigger point: manually with a "review PR" command or automatically in CI on every PR.
Agree that the agent's output is a comment in the PR, input for a human, not an auto-block on merge.
Run the agent on 3-5 real PRs and compare findings against the expert's opinion.
Calibrate the checklist by results: what the agent missed — add, what's noise — remove.
Remember the boundary from step 1: the final decision and architecture stay with the human.
s6.validate: The agent runs on new PRs, and the expert confirms the findings save them time without creating noise.
s6.tip: Every couple of weeks revisit the checklist based on fresh findings — it's a living document, not a stone.

agent-audit.title: Build an Audit Agent
agent-audit.subtitle: An agent that takes material and produces an audit by fixed criteria
agent-audit.whatItIs:
An Audit Agent is an [[node:agents|agent]] that takes input material (a screen, a text, a process) and returns a structured audit: a list of findings sorted by impact, each with a severity level and a recommendation. Not a "general opinion", but a check against a pre-fixed checklist of criteria.

The core idea is that the criteria are fixed in advance, not invented on the fly. Then two runs on similar material give comparable results, and reports can be compared over time. The agent is especially strong paired with [[node:mcp|MCP]] to the relevant system and topical [[node:skills|Skills]] that hold the criteria and reference standards.
agent-audit.approach: Don't ask "is this good" — that yields a vague answer. First fix the criteria and the report format, and only then run the audit. An auditor's strength is not the model's cleverness but the clarity of the frame you give it.
outcomes: Understand where an audit agent is genuinely useful and where it gives false confidence
Can fix a set of criteria so the audit is reproducible
Write a role-and-input prompt that keeps the agent from drifting
Get a report in "finding + severity + recommendation" format, ready to act on
Calibrate criteria after the first run and remove noisy findings

applyIn.title: UX audit of a screen
applyIn.description: Before release, run a mockup or page against a heuristics checklist and get a prioritized list of top problems — without waiting for a full test with people.

applyIn.title: Content audit
applyIn.description: An article, landing page or email is checked against criteria for clarity, structure and tone of voice. The agent catches weak spots before the editor does.

applyIn.title: Process or document audit
applyIn.description: A policy, onboarding checklist or spec is run for completeness and contradictions against fixed rules.

pitfalls: Using the agent to replace checks with real users — the agent has hypotheses, people have facts
Criteria on the fly: without a fixed checklist, two runs produce different findings
Asking it to "find everything" — the agent returns noise; limit to top-N by impact
A report without severity and recommendation — a problem list nobody prioritizes
Blindly trusting conclusions without calibrating on material where you know the right answer

exercises.question: Take one real piece of material (a screen, article or policy) and write 5 criteria worth checking it against. Phrase each as a verifiable statement.
exercises.hint: If a criterion can't be answered yes/no or scored on a scale, it's too vague — rephrase it.

exercises.question: Run the Audit Agent on this material with your criteria and require the "finding + severity + recommendation" format. Then sort the findings yourself and compare with the agent's order.
exercises.hint: A mismatch in priorities signals that the severity criterion is described unclearly.

exercises.question: Feed the agent material where you already know the weak spot. Check whether it found it and didn't invent extras.
exercises.hint: A missed known problem or a false finding is a reason to calibrate the criteria, not to trust the run.

s1.title: Understand why an audit agent and where it applies
s1.why: Without a clear application area the auditor either duplicates manual work or creates false confidence where live users are needed.
instructions: Write down what material you check regularly: screens, texts, processes, specs.
Note where there's no time for a full manual audit but you need a quick "is it okay?" signal.
Honestly separate tasks where the agent gives hypotheses (UX, text clarity) from tasks needing facts from people (real behavior).
Pick ONE material type for your first auditor — don't try to cover everything at once.
s1.validate: You have one concrete material type and one sentence: "why I need an auditor here".
s1.tip: The best first candidate is something you check often and by the same rules. That's where the payback is highest.

s2.title: Fix the audit criteria
s2.why: Fixed criteria are the audit itself. Without them the agent scores differently each time, and runs can't be compared.
instructions: Write 5–8 criteria for the chosen material. Each is a verifiable statement, not a wish.
Phrase criteria so the answer is "met / violated / not applicable", not "fine".
Add to each criterion a short reference or example of a violation — the agent relies on it.
Group criteria by theme (e.g. clarity, structure, accessibility) so the report reads well.
Store the criteria separately (in a [[node:skills|Skill]] or file) — this is a reusable frame, not part of a one-off prompt.
s2.validate: The criteria list reads such that another person could check the same material against it and reach a similar conclusion.
s2.tip: If a criterion can't be checked by looking at the material alone, it's not an audit criterion but a question for user research.

s3.title: Set the agent's role and input format
s3.why: A clear role and predictable input keep the agent from drifting into general reasoning instead of checking against criteria.
instructions: Describe the role: "You are an auditor of <material type>, check strictly against the given criteria, add none of your own."
Pass the criteria from step 2 into the prompt or connect them via a [[node:skills|Skill]].
Fix what is given as input: one screen / one article / one document per run, not a batch at once.
Forbid the agent from evaluating anything not in the criteria — otherwise you get taste-based judgments.
Follow the [[node:ag-principles|agent principles]]: one clear task, explicit input, explicit output.
s3.validate: The prompt describes the role, lists the criteria and unambiguously states what counts as input.
s3.tip: One run — one object. Feed ten screens at once and the agent will mix findings and lose accuracy.

s4.title: Define the report format: finding + severity + recommendation
s4.why: A report without structure is a wall of text nobody prioritizes. A strict format makes the audit immediately actionable.
instructions: Require every finding to contain three fields: what's wrong, severity level, what to do.
Fix the severity scale: e.g. critical / major / minor — and explain to the agent what each level means.
Ask it to sort findings by impact and limit to top-N (e.g. top-7), not dump everything.
Add to each finding a reference to its criterion from step 2 — so it's clear which rule is violated.
End the report with a short summary: "all okay / there are blockers" — that's the quick signal.
s4.validate: Any finding can be read and instantly understood: how serious it is and what to do about it.
s4.tip: Severity without a defined scale is useless — the agent will assign levels at random. Describe what separates critical from minor.

s5.title: Run the audit on real material
s5.why: Only a live run shows whether the criteria and format work, or whether the agent finds noise and misses what matters.
instructions: Take real material, not a textbook example — preferably something you're about to release.
Run the agent and get a report in the step 4 format.
Read the findings top to bottom: do you agree with the impact order?
Mark findings that turned out to be noise, and important things the agent missed.
If you have [[node:mcp|MCP]] access to the system, let the agent pull the material directly rather than copying by hand.
s5.validate: You hold a report on real material plus notes on where the agent hit and where it missed.
s5.tip: The first run is almost always noisy. That's normal — it's there to show which criteria to calibrate.

s6.title: Calibrate criteria and check for mistakes
s6.why: The auditor becomes reliable only after calibration: without it you mass-produce noise and false confidence.
instructions: Remove or rephrase criteria that produced noisy findings in step 5.
Refine the severity definitions if the agent's priorities diverged from yours.
Run the agent on material where you know the right answer — check for misses and inventions.
Encode the agent's frequent mistakes into the criteria as explicit bans ("don't flag X as a problem").
Save the final version of the criteria in a [[node:skills|Skill]] — now the audit is reproducible and reusable.
s6.validate: A repeat run on familiar material gives a stable, clear report with no obvious noise and no missed known problems.
s6.tip: Remember the boundary: an audit agent gives hypotheses by criteria, but does not replace checks with real users — they have the facts.

agent-researcher.title: Research agent: from question to a report with references
agent-researcher.subtitle: Build an agent that finds sources, synthesizes them, and delivers a verifiable report
agent-researcher.whatItIs: A research agent is an [[node:agents|agent]] that, given a question, searches sources online on its own, reads them, compares facts, and returns a structured report with quotes and links. It does not replace an analyst — it removes the routine: reading dozens of pages, note-taking, and formatting references.
agent-researcher.approach: The course is built around the main risk of such an agent — making up facts and links. So every step serves one goal: any conclusion in the report must be traceable to a real source. First we set boundaries and frame the question, then connect web search, synthesize with citations, separately verify key facts, and only then assemble the report.
outcomes: Understand where a research agent helps and where its conclusions can't be trusted without checking
Frame a research question and criteria for selecting sources
Connect web search and tools so the agent works with real data
Get a synthesis where every claim is tied to a link
Verify key facts and produce a reproducible report

applyIn.title: Competitor analysis
applyIn.description: The agent gathers competitors' prices, features, and positioning from public sources and compiles a comparison table with links to the originals.

applyIn.title: Market overview before launch
applyIn.description: Before a product launch the agent prepares a segment overview: market size, trends, key players — noting where each figure came from.

applyIn.title: Decision prep
applyIn.description: For an internal memo or pitch the agent finds and organizes facts, saving hours of manual googling and note-taking.

pitfalls: Trusting conclusions without checking sources: the model can invent a plausible but non-existent link
Asking too broad a question — the agent returns a shallow report about everything and nothing
Not setting source criteria: the agent mixes fresh data with a five-year-old article
Accepting synthesis without citations: you can't tell a sourced fact from the model's guess
Skipping verification of key figures — one wrong number ruins the whole report

exercises.question: The agent delivered a report where the claim "the market grew 40%" has a link, but the page doesn't open. What is this and what do you do?
exercises.hint: Recall the main risk from step 1: the model can generate plausible but non-existent links. Every key figure needs its own check (step 5).

exercises.question: The question is "tell me about the AI tools market." Why will the agent give a weak result and how do you reframe it?
exercises.hint: Too broad. Narrow it to a concrete slice: segment, region, period, what exactly you're comparing (see step 2 — question + criteria).

exercises.question: How do you make the final report re-checkable a month later?
exercises.hint: Think reproducibility: record the search date, direct links, verbatim quotes, and the original question wording (step 6).

s1.title: Why a research agent and where its limits are
s1.why: Before building the agent it's important to understand its strength and weakness. The strength is speed of gathering and synthesis. The weakness is a tendency to [[node:cap-limitations|hallucinate]]: the model can confidently produce a fact or link that doesn't exist. Ignore this and the report will look convincing yet be wrong.
instructions: Define which routine you want to remove: reading, note-taking, formatting references
Write down what decisions will be based on the report and the cost of an error
Adopt the rule: no conclusion goes into the report without a verifiable source
Define the distrust zone — figures, dates, quotes always require verification
s1.validate: You can explain in one sentence why the agent can't be trusted without checking links.
s1.tip: The higher the cost of a wrong decision, the stricter the verification in step 5 must be.

s2.title: Frame the question and source criteria
s2.why: Report quality is set by question quality. A broad question ("tell me about the market") yields a shallow answer. A narrow question with source-selection criteria steers the agent to the right data and cuts the noise.
instructions: Narrow the topic to a concrete slice: segment, region, period, object of comparison
Break the main question into 2–4 sub-questions answerable with a fact
Set source criteria: recency, type (official/news/research), language
Describe which sources don't qualify (forums, ads, undated content)
s2.validate: You have one narrow question, 2–4 sub-questions, and an explicit list of source criteria.
s2.tip: A good test of a question: it can be answered with a table or list of facts, not an essay.

s3.title: Connect web search and tools
s3.why: Without access to external data the agent relies only on the model's memory, which is stale and incomplete. [[node:cap-search|Web search]] gives the agent real sources in real time — turning guesses into verifiable facts.
instructions: Enable the web search tool for the agent and, if needed, a page-reading tool
Check that the agent returns not just text but the URL of each source
Set the rule: find sources first, then draw conclusions, not the other way around
Limit the number of sources per sub-question to avoid drowning in noise
s3.validate: A test run returns real links that open, not general reasoning.
s3.tip: If the agent answers without links, the tool isn't connected or isn't being used — check the configuration.

s4.title: Synthesis with citations and links
s4.why: The agent's main value is not retelling individual pages but synthesis: comparing sources and drawing patterns. But synthesis without links is useless — you can't tell a fact from a guess. The principle of [[node:ag-principles|transparency]] requires every claim to be traceable to a source.
instructions: Ask the agent to group facts by sub-question, not by source
Every claim must be accompanied by a link to its source
When sources conflict — show both, don't silently pick one
Quote exact figures and citations precisely, without paraphrasing
s4.validate: In the synthesis draft every fact has a link next to it, and conflicts aren't hidden.
s4.tip: A footnote like "claim [source]" beats a list of links at the end — it's easier to verify.

s5.title: Verifying key facts
s5.why: This is the step that separates research from a nice retelling. Even with search connected, the model can attach a wrong link to a fact or distort a figure. Key facts are checked separately — by following the link and comparing.
instructions: Pick 3–5 facts that the report's conclusions rest on
Check each link: does it open and does it contain the claimed fact
Compare figures and dates verbatim with the original source
Mark anything unverified as a hypothesis, not a fact
If a source isn't confirmed — drop the claim or find another
s5.validate: All key figures and quotes are confirmed by working links; anything unverified is clearly marked.
s5.tip: Start verifying with the loudest, most surprising figures — those are exactly what the model distorts most often.

s6.title: Report format, common mistakes, and final check
s6.why: The report must be not only correct but reproducible: a month later it should be clear where each conclusion came from. A good format and a final checklist lock in the discipline built in the previous steps.
instructions: Structure the report: question → brief conclusion → facts with sources → table/comparison → list of links
Record the search date and the original question wording
Run the checklist: every fact has a link, key figures are verified, conflicts are shown
Separate the agent's opinion from source facts in a dedicated block
Save the report so it can be re-checked later
s6.validate: The report reads in minutes, every conclusion traces to a source, the checklist is fully passed.
s6.tip: Final question to yourself: "could another person reproduce this research from the report?" If not — add the missing links and date.

agent-designer.title: Designer Assistant
agent-designer.subtitle: A design-critic agent: reviews, UX copy, component variants, and accessibility checks
agent-designer.whatItIs: Designer Assistant is an on-demand [[node:agents|agent]] that acts as a designer's partner: it gives structured critique of a layout, writes and edits UX copy, suggests component variants, and checks the design for accessibility. It is not an image generator and not a substitute for taste — it is a second pair of eyes that catches problems by heuristics and offers alternatives.
agent-designer.approach: The course builds the agent around a clear role and context (brand, guide, audience), four working modes (critique, UX copy, variants, accessibility), input rules (screenshot or text description), and a strict output format — concrete edits instead of vague words. It ends with embedding the agent into the team's workflow and common pitfalls. Grounded in [[node:ag-principles|agent principles]] and [[node:cap-input-modalities|input modalities]].
outcomes: You understand where a design assistant helps and where its output cannot be trusted
You can set a role, brand context, and audience so the critique is relevant
You switch the agent between four modes: critique, UX copy, variants, accessibility
You get concrete edits with location and reason on output, not generic advice
You embed the agent into the iteration loop before handing off to development (handoff)

applyIn.title: Solo layout review
applyIn.description: When a fellow designer is busy, the agent gives a fast structured breakdown of a screen: hierarchy, contrast, spacing, states.

applyIn.title: Refining interface text
applyIn.description: Buttons, errors, empty states, onboarding — in UX-copy mode the agent rewrites wording to match brand tone and audience.

applyIn.title: Pre-handoff check
applyIn.description: Before passing to development, the agent runs an accessibility check and notes what to fix while it's still cheap.

pitfalls: Expecting artistic taste from the agent — it's strong in heuristics and rules, not aesthetics
Giving input without context (brand, audience, screen goal) — the critique comes out generic and useless
Accepting "looks good" as an answer — without demanding concrete edits the agent just rambles
Relying on the accessibility output as a formal audit — it's a hint, not a WCAG certificate
Mixing the four modes in one request — answers get blurry, separate the tasks

exercises.question: Why shouldn't a design assistant be trusted with the final aesthetic judgment of a layout?
exercises.hint: Recall where the agent is strong (heuristics, rules, accessibility) and where its boundary lies.

exercises.question: Why is "weak hierarchy here, raise the heading to 24px and add 16px spacing" better than "looks fine"?
exercises.hint: Think about the output-format step: specific location + specific edit + reason.

exercises.question: Why split the modes (critique / UX copy / variants / accessibility) into separate requests?
exercises.hint: What happens to focus and answer quality when the agent tries to do everything at once?

s1.title: Why a design assistant and where its limits are
s1.why: Without a clear goal and boundaries, the agent becomes a generator of pretty but empty advice. First we fix what it can really do — and what not to trust.
instructions: State one sentence: "This agent helps me with critique, copy, variants, and accessibility during iteration."
Write the boundary explicitly: the agent is strong in heuristics and rules but does not judge artistic taste and does not replace the designer's final call.
Define the stage it kicks in — research and iteration, before handing off to development (handoff).
Decide what you do NOT expect from it: final image generation, brand decisions, legal review.
s1.validate: You have one sentence about its value and one explicit list of what not to trust.
s1.tip: The boundary matters more than the capabilities: teams break trust in the agent exactly where they overestimate it.

s2.title: Set the role and context: brand, guide, audience
s2.why: Critique without context is always generic. Brand, tone, and audience turn abstract advice into a relevant edit for your product.
instructions: Describe the role: "You are a senior product designer reviewing our product's screens."
Give brand context: tone of voice, key colors, fonts, a link to or summary of the design guide.
Describe the audience: who the user is, their level, the usage context (mobile/desktop, rushed/thoughtful).
Fix the screen goal: what the user should accomplish here — this is the yardstick for all critique.
Reference [[node:ag-principles|agent principles]] so the role and context stay stable across requests.
s2.validate: The agent's system description has a role, brand context, audience, and screen goal.
s2.tip: If there's no guide — ask the agent to first output 5 assumed principles and confirm them.

s3.title: Four modes: critique, UX copy, variants, accessibility
s3.why: One agent covers four different tasks. Explicit modes keep answers focused and predictable.
instructions: "Critique" mode: the agent gives N observations on hierarchy, contrast, spacing, states — with priority.
"UX copy" mode: rewrites interface text to match brand tone — buttons, errors, empty states.
"Variants" mode: offers 2-3 alternatives of a component or layout with pros and cons of each.
"Accessibility" mode: checks contrast, touch-target sizes, alt text, focus order.
Agree to invoke modes one per request, not all at once — this keeps focus.
s3.validate: Each of the four modes has its own invocation phrasing and a clear expected result.
s3.tip: Name the mode in words at the start of the request ("Mode: critique") — the agent holds the frame better.

s4.title: Input: screenshot or description
s4.why: The quality of the review depends directly on what and how you feed the agent. Image and text work differently.
instructions: A screenshot is the best input for critique and accessibility: real hierarchy, contrast, and spacing are visible.
If there's no image — give a structural description: which blocks, in what order, the texts, the states.
Always attach the screen goal and the key scenario — without them the critique hangs in the air.
Check against [[node:cap-input-modalities|input modalities]]: make sure the agent can accept an image.
For UX copy, give the current wording verbatim — the agent edits the concrete, not the imagined.
s4.validate: You know which input format to give for each mode and you always attach the screen goal.
s4.tip: One screen, one input. Don't dump five screenshots into one request for a "general overview."

s5.title: Output format: concrete edits, not vague words
s5.why: "Looks fine" is useless. The agent's value is in edits you can apply immediately: location, change, reason.
instructions: Demand a template: each edit = [location] + [concrete change] + [why].
Forbid judgment phrases without action ("nice", "clean", "modern").
Ask for priority: critical / nice-to-have / later — so you know what to tackle first.
For variants, require pros and cons of each, not a single "correct" answer.
Cap the volume: 5 observations + 3 ideas beat 30 unprioritized points.
s5.validate: Any agent answer can be taken and applied to the layout without guessing what it meant.
s5.tip: Add a "how to verify it improved" field to the format — this turns critique into something measurable.

s6.title: Embedding into the workflow, pitfalls, and verification
s6.why: The agent is only useful if it's embedded into a real iteration loop and the team understands its weak spots.
instructions: Define call points: after the first sketch, before the team review, before handoff.
Tie the accessibility mode to the final check — it's cheaper to fix before development.
Fix the pitfalls: don't expect taste, don't give input without context, don't mix modes.
Lean on the [[node:ai-native-design|AI-native approach]] — the agent is part of the process, not a one-off trick.
Once per sprint, verify the agent's output actually helps rather than creating noise.
s6.validate: The team has clear points where the agent is invoked and a shared list of its limitations.
s6.tip: Save successful prompts as templates — this turns a one-off win into a repeatable process.

agent-pm.title: PM Assistant
agent-pm.subtitle: User stories, acceptance criteria, task breakdown, and release prep
agent-pm.whatItIs:
A PM Assistant is an [[node:agents|agent]] that takes formulation routine off the product manager: it turns a raw idea into a user story, writes acceptance criteria, breaks a large task into clear subtasks, and assembles a changelog for the release.

It's important to understand the boundary: the agent speeds up documenting what you've already decided. It doesn't run stakeholder interviews, doesn't prioritize the backlog for you, and doesn't make product decisions. The final "yes" always belongs to a human — the agent prepares a draft, the human reviews it and takes responsibility.
agent-pm.approach: Don't try to automate product thinking. Give the agent clear product context and a role, feed it concrete statements, and read every result critically. The best mode is "the agent writes a draft in a minute, you refine it in five," not "the agent decides and you agree."
outcomes: Turn an idea into a correct user story in minutes instead of half an hour
Write verifiable acceptance criteria so the team and QA know what "done" means
Break a large task into right-sized subtasks without losing meaning
Prepare a clean changelog and release notes from a list of changes
Keep a single backlog format across the whole team

applyIn.title: Backlog grooming
applyIn.description: Before a sprint, run raw tickets through the agent — you get uniform user stories with AC, ready for the team to estimate.

applyIn.title: Epic decomposition
applyIn.description: The agent breaks a large feature into subtasks with dependencies and risks; you adjust the order and hand it to engineering.

applyIn.title: Release prep
applyIn.description: From the list of merged changes, the agent assembles a changelog and release notes for both users and the team.

pitfalls: Replacing stakeholder interviews with generation: the agent's hypotheses ≠ real user needs.
Accepting acceptance criteria you can't verify ("should be convenient") — that's not an AC.
Splitting tasks endlessly: 15 micro-tickets for a simple feature is noise, not clarity.
Trusting the agent to prioritize the backlog — that's a human product decision.
Copying the changelog to production without proofreading: the agent may invent an item that wasn't in the commits.

exercises.question: Take a real one-line feature idea and ask the agent to return a user story in the format "As a <role>, I want <action>, so that <value>." Check that the role and value aren't made up.
exercises.hint: If the value is a generic "so it's better," send it back: the value should be measurable or concrete.

exercises.question: Ask the agent to turn one user story into acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then format. Try to "fail" at least one criterion yourself — find the gap.
exercises.hint: A good AC can be unambiguously marked as passed or not. If a criterion can be argued over, it's poorly worded.

exercises.question: Give the agent 5–7 lines of "what changed in the release" and ask it to group them into a changelog by section (New / Fixed / Changed).
exercises.hint: Check each item against the source list — there should be no extra items.

s1.title: Why a PM Assistant and where its boundary is
s1.why: Before configuring the agent, it's important to nail down what it does and doesn't do. Otherwise it's easy to slide into the agent "deciding" for the product while the human just agrees. The PM Assistant speeds up documentation, but the decision and the responsibility stay with the human.
instructions: Write out 3–4 routine operations that take your time: drafting user stories, AC, breakdown, changelog.
Next to them, note what the agent must not do: user interviews, prioritization, product decisions.
Set a rule for yourself: every agent result is a draft you review, not a final answer.
Look into the [[node:ag-principles|agent principles]] to understand how responsibility is split between human and agent.
s1.validate: You have two short lists — "the agent does" and "the agent doesn't" — and you understand why the final decision belongs to a human.
s1.tip: If a task requires understanding a real user need, that's a signal you need an interview, not generation.

s2.title: Set the role and product context
s2.why: Without product context the agent writes generic, faceless wording. The more precisely it knows the product, who the users are, and the team's conventions, the less you'll have to rewrite after it.
instructions: Set the role: "You are an experienced PM Assistant who helps document the backlog."
Describe the product in 3–5 sentences: what it is, who it's for, key scenarios.
List the user types (roles) — you'll need them for user stories.
Fix the team conventions: user story format, AC format (e.g., Given/When/Then), subtask size.
Connect the context to how an [[node:ai-native-product|AI-native product]] is built, if that applies to your case.
s2.validate: In response, the agent can restate in its own words what the product is, who the users are, and in what format it will deliver results.
s2.tip: Save this context block separately and reuse it in every session — don't re-explain the product each time.

s3.title: User stories from an idea
s3.why: A user story translates a raw idea into the language of the user and their value. This protects the team from building a feature "just because we felt like it," without understanding who needs it and why.
instructions: Give the agent the idea statement in 1–2 lines.
Ask it to return a user story in the format "As a <role>, I want <action>, so that <value>."
Require that the role comes from your user list, not an invented one.
Ask for 1–2 clarifying questions if the agent lacks data — instead of guessing.
Check the value: it should explain "why," not repeat "what."
s3.validate: The user story reads from the perspective of a specific user, the value answers "why," and it contains no invented details.
s3.tip: If the agent produces a value like "to make it more convenient," ask it to be specific: what exactly becomes faster, cheaper, or clearer.

s4.title: Acceptance criteria and breaking into tasks
s4.why: Acceptance criteria turn a story into a verifiable "done": both the developer and QA understand the same way when the task is closed. Breakdown, in turn, makes the work estimable and keeps it from dragging on for weeks.
instructions: Ask the agent to write acceptance criteria for the user story in Given/When/Then format.
Require that each criterion be verifiable: unambiguously "passed" or "not."
Ask it to separately list edge and negative cases (errors, empty data, access rights).
Then ask it to break the story into subtasks sized so each closes within 1–2 days.
Clarify dependencies between subtasks and risks — what could go wrong.
s4.validate: Each AC can be objectively marked as passed, and the subtasks fully cover the story and have a clear size.
s4.tip: Reword any criterion that allows an argument over "does this count as done or not?" until the argument disappears.

s5.title: Release prep and changelog
s5.why: The release is where the product meets the user. A clean changelog saves support and team time and tells the user what changed for them. The agent quickly assembles a draft from the list of changes.
instructions: Collect the list of changes that went into the release (from closed tasks or commits).
Ask the agent to group them into sections: New / Fixed / Changed / Known issues.
Ask for two versions: a technical one for the team and a clear one for users.
Require each changelog item to rely on the source list — no invented lines.
Add a brief 1–2 sentence release summary for the announcement.
s5.validate: The changelog is split into sections, each item is backed by the source list, and there's a separate clear version for users.
s5.tip: Before publishing, compare the changelog against the change list line by line — that's the main source of "phantom" items.

s6.title: Output format, common mistakes, and verification
s6.why: For the agent's results to drop straight into your tool (Jira, Linear, Notion), you need a stable output format. And for the agent to bring value rather than risk, you need a short habit of checking every result.
instructions: Fix the output format: e.g., title, user story, AC block, subtask list, risks.
Ask the agent to always deliver in this format so it can be copied without rework.
Add a list of common mistakes to the instruction: unverifiable AC, invented roles, phantom changelog items.
Introduce a final check: you read the result and confirm the roles are real, the AC verifiable, nothing extra.
Check against the [[node:ag-principles|agent principles]] — the human confirms the result before it goes into work.
s6.validate: The agent reliably delivers results in one format, and you have a short verification checklist that you actually apply to every answer.
s6.tip: Save the format and the mistake list right in the agent's system instruction — then they apply automatically in every session.

agent-managed.title: Claude Managed Agents: Anthropic's managed agent harness
agent-managed.subtitle: Ready-made infrastructure for long-running async agents — without your own DevOps
agent-managed.whatItIs:
Managed Agents is an official Anthropic product: a ready-made, configurable agent harness running in managed cloud infrastructure. Instead of building an agent loop from scratch (retries, timeouts, state, observability), you submit a task, the agent runs asynchronously, and you poll for the result.

It's a layer on top of [[node:agents|agents]]: the same [[node:ag-principles|agent loop principles]], but execution, state, and tools are handled by the platform. This course shows when to pick the ready-made option and when to build your own via the [[node:pl-api|API]].
agent-managed.approach: Don't reach for Managed Agents on every task. It's a tool for long, asynchronous, production workloads that need reliability. For a simple one-shot request the Messages API directly is enough. First honestly assess task duration and reliability requirements — then choose the layer.
outcomes: Understand what Managed Agents are and how they differ from a self-built agent harness
Know exactly what the platform handles: execution, state, tools, observability
Can submit a first task and poll for the result
Can configure an agent for a specific task via tools and parameters
Understand limits, the cost model, and where your control remains

applyIn.title: Long-running research tasks
applyIn.description: "Research this topic and write a report" — the agent runs for minutes or hours, uses web search and file tools, returns a structured result.

applyIn.title: Production agent deployments
applyIn.description: When an agent must run reliably under load and you have no time to build retries and observability yourself.

applyIn.title: Asynchronous pipelines
applyIn.description: Submit a task, do other work, collect the result later. Fits background processing where instant responses aren't needed.

pitfalls: Using Managed Agents for simple single-turn tasks — it's overkill; calling the Messages API directly is cheaper and simpler.
Expecting a synchronous reply: the model is async — submit the task and poll for the result, don't wait inside one call.
Launching long tasks without understanding cost — a long agent loop burns more tokens than it seems.
Assuming the platform removes all responsibility: you still define the task, the tools, and verify the result.
Choosing the ready-made harness where full loop customization is needed — building your own via the API would be more precise.

exercises.question: Frame one task that genuinely benefits from Managed Agents (long + async + needs reliability) and one for which it would be overkill. Explain the difference.
exercises.hint: A long research task with web search versus a one-shot "rephrase this paragraph". Lean on the criterion: task duration and reliability requirement.

exercises.question: Describe what you'd have to build yourself if Managed Agents didn't exist: list at least four harness elements.
exercises.hint: Recall what the platform handles out of the box: retries, timeouts, state storage, observability.

exercises.question: For your own task decide: Managed Agents, a self-built agent on the [[node:pl-api|API]], or a simple Messages API call? Justify it.
exercises.hint: One-shot and simple → Messages API. Long and standard → Managed Agents. Long with a non-standard loop → your own agent.

s1.title: What Managed Agents are and when to pick them over your own harness
s1.why: Before adopting the product you need to understand the exact problem it solves. Managed Agents close out weeks of work building a reliable agent loop — but only for a specific class of tasks.
instructions: Memorize the definition: a ready-made, configurable agent harness in Anthropic's managed cloud infrastructure.
Fix the selection criterion: long tasks (minutes to hours), asynchronous work, production reliability.
Compare with the alternative: building the loop yourself via the [[node:pl-api|API]] — retries, timeouts, state, observability — which takes weeks.
Note the boundary: for a simple one-shot request use the Messages API directly, not Managed Agents.
s1.validate: You can name three signs of a task where Managed Agents are the right choice, and one sign where they're overkill.
s1.tip: If you're unsure whether a task runs longer than a minute, that alone hints toward managed asynchronous execution.

s2.title: What the platform handles: execution, state, tools
s2.why: The value of Managed Agents is exactly what gets taken off your plate. Knowing this list answers why weeks of work turn into hours.
instructions: Execution: the platform runs the agent loop itself — running steps, handling retries and timeouts.
State: progress of a long task is stored on the platform side, you don't keep it yourself.
Tools: the agent has built-in tools — web search and file operations — without separate integration.
Observability: you can track task progress by polling its status and result.
Map each item to what you'd otherwise have to write yourself via the [[node:pl-api|API]].
s2.validate: You can list at least four things Managed Agents do for you, and for each name what it saves.
s2.tip: The built-in web search and file tools are the same ones [[node:agents|agents]] use, just without your setup.

s3.title: How to start: submit a task and poll for the result
s3.why: The model of work is asynchronous, and that's the key difference from a regular request. You need to grasp the "submit — agent runs — poll" cycle before any configuration.
instructions: Frame the task as a clear goal, e.g. "research this topic and write a report".
Submit the task to the agent — the call returns a job identifier, not a finished answer.
Give the agent time to work: it uses the available tools and goes through the loop steps itself.
Poll for the result by identifier — when the task is done you get structured output.
Don't expect an instant reply in one call — this is an asynchronous model.
s3.validate: You understand the three phases — submit task, agent runs, poll result — and why the answer doesn't come back synchronously.
s3.tip: Frame the task as carefully as a regular prompt: the clearer the goal and result format, the more precisely the agent works.

s4.title: Configuring for the task: tools and parameters
s4.why: The harness is ready-made but configurable. For a specific task it pays to narrow or steer the agent — that improves the result and cuts unnecessary steps.
instructions: Decide which tools the task needs: web search only, files only, or both.
Frame the task with an explicit result format so the output is structured.
Give the agent instructions the same way you describe a regular [[node:agents|agent]]'s behavior.
Test on a small task before launching a long one — that's a cheaper way to catch wording flaws.
s4.validate: You've configured an agent for your task: picked the needed tools and described the expected result format.
s4.tip: The narrower the tool and goal wording, the fewer extra steps the agent takes — and the cheaper the run.

s5.title: Limits, cost, and where your control remains
s5.why: A long agent loop burns more tokens than a one-off call. Without understanding cost it's easy to get an unexpected bill, and without understanding control it's easy to lose grip on the task.
instructions: Remember: a long task = many steps = more tokens than a single Messages API request.
Start with short tasks to estimate real cost before launching multi-hour ones.
Control stays with you: you set the goal, pick the tools, and verify the final result.
Poll the status to follow progress and catch early if the task drifts off course.
Don't launch expensive long tasks blindly — first run a simplified version.
s5.validate: You understand why a long agent costs more than a one-off call, and can name what in the task stays under your control.
s5.tip: Treat the first run of a long task as a cost measurement, not as the final result.

s6.title: When Managed Agents are NOT a fit + final check
s6.why: The most common mistake is applying a powerful tool to the wrong place. Clear understanding of the boundaries matters as much as understanding the capabilities.
instructions: Simple one-shot task → the Messages API directly; Managed Agents are overkill.
Need an instant synchronous reply → the asynchronous model doesn't fit.
Need full customization of the agent loop → build your own agent on the [[node:pl-api|API]] following the [[node:ag-principles|agent loop principles]].
Need non-standard tools beyond the built-ins → check whether web search and files are enough, otherwise look toward [[node:mcp|MCP]] and your own harness.
Check your task against all the signs and make a deliberate decision.
s6.validate: You can make a reasoned choice for a specific task between Managed Agents, a self-built API agent, and a simple Messages API call.
s6.tip: If none of the criteria "long + async + reliability" hold, you almost certainly need a plain API call, not Managed Agents.

cap-input-modalities.title: Input modalities: what Claude accepts as input
cap-input-modalities.subtitle: An overview course on input channels — text, documents, images, files — and how to combine them in a single request
cap-input-modalities.whatItIs: Claude isn't just a "text chatter" — it's a multi-modal system. It accepts more than text on input: images, PDFs, spreadsheets, CSV, JSON and other files. This course maps every input channel and teaches you to pick the right one for the task. Deep dives into individual modalities live in the [[node:cap-vision|Vision]] and [[node:cap-files|Files]] courses; the overall capability map is in [[node:capabilities|Capabilities]].
cap-input-modalities.approach: We move from the big-picture map to the details and then to combining. First we cover which inputs are supported and why; then, one by one — text and large documents, images, files/PDF; then we learn to stitch several modalities into one request; finally — the limits of what's possible and the common mistakes, with a check. Each step gives a concrete selection rule, not theory.
outcomes: You know all of Claude's input channels and which one fits which task
You can decide when text is enough and when you need a file or image
You understand the Vision-vs-Files difference and don't overpay for image tokens
You can assemble a request from several modalities (e.g., screenshot + PDF + text)
You know the limits: what Claude won't accept and what needs preprocessing

applyIn.title: Document processing
applyIn.description: Invoices, contracts, reports arrive as PDFs and scans. Knowing modalities lets you extract data without retyping by hand.

applyIn.title: Interface and design analysis
applyIn.description: UX screenshots, mockups, charts — Claude reads layout and composition directly via Vision, no word-by-word description needed.

applyIn.title: Designing AI workflows
applyIn.description: Real tasks are almost always multi-modal. The input map helps you design a flow that doesn't lose data.

pitfalls: Converting everything to text before the request — you lose PDF layout and image composition
Using Vision where Files would do: a screenshot of a PDF page is more expensive and worse than parsing its text layer
Assuming Claude only works in chat — ignoring files and images means losing 60-70% of its capabilities
Loading an entire huge document when you only need a fragment — it bloats context and cost
Not checking that the input actually arrived and was recognized — Claude silently works with whatever it got

exercises.question: Your inputs are: a scanned invoice (PDF), a phone photo of a receipt, and a question about the current tax rate. Which modalities do you use and why?
exercises.hint: A scanned PDF and a photo are different channels. Think about what reads an image best vs. what reads document structure. The tax rate is knowledge outside your files.

exercises.question: You're sent a PDF report with a real text layer. Upload it as a file or as page screenshots? Justify your choice.
exercises.hint: Compare accuracy and cost. The text layer is already machine-readable — do you need to turn it into a picture?

exercises.question: Name an input Claude will NOT accept directly, and suggest how to prepare it.
exercises.hint: Think about audio and video. What do you need to do to a call recording before Claude can work with it?

s1.title: Which inputs are supported and why
s1.why: Without an overall map of inputs, you default to text only and lose most of the capability. This step sets the frame for the whole course.
instructions: Write down the four input channels: text, images, files, web search
Open [[node:capabilities|Capabilities]] and match each channel to a real task from your work
Remember the rule: if you send only text and get only text, that's 30-40% of the capability
Note that some inputs require special processing modes (citations from documents, running code)
s1.validate: You can name at least three tasks from your work where the input is a file or image, not text.
s1.tip: Don't memorize processing modes at this step — lock in the input channels themselves first.

s2.title: Text and large documents
s2.why: Text is the base channel, but it has a limit: you can't blindly paste a very large document whole. You need to know when text is enough and when sending a file is cheaper.
instructions: For short requests and instructions, use plain text in the chat
For a medium document, paste the text directly and clearly separate it from the question
For a very large document, don't paste it all — send it as a file and ask for the relevant fragment
State the task on the text explicitly: what to extract, in what format to return it
s2.validate: You understand the point at which pasting text becomes worse than uploading a file.
s2.tip: The more precisely you specify what you need from the document, the less context is wasted.

s3.title: Images
s3.why: Screenshots, photos, charts and mockups carry information text can't convey: layout, color, composition. Claude reads them directly via Vision.
instructions: Use images for interface screenshots, photos, diagrams and design mockups
Static formats are supported: PNG, JPG, WebP, GIF
Pose a concrete question about the picture: what to find, compare, or extract
For a deep dive into capabilities and limits, open the [[node:cap-vision|Vision]] course
s3.validate: You can explain why a chart screenshot is better sent as an image than described in words.
s3.tip: Images cost more than text (image tokens) — don't send a picture where text or a file would do.

s4.title: Files and PDF
s4.why: Most real data arrives as files: PDF, DOCX, XLSX, CSV, JSON. Sending a file preserves structure and is often more accurate and cheaper than a screenshot.
instructions: Send structured documents as files: PDF, spreadsheets, CSV, JSON
If a PDF has a text layer, send it as a file, not as page screenshots
For tabular data and calculations, a file is more accurate than a picture of the table
For a deep dive into formats and scenarios, see the [[node:cap-files|Files]] course and the [[node:p-files|working with files]] node
s4.validate: You choose between a file and an image deliberately, based on the presence of a text layer and structure.
s4.tip: A PDF with a text layer is almost always better as a file than a screenshot: cheaper and free of recognition errors.

s5.title: How to combine modalities in one request
s5.why: Real tasks are rarely single-modal. Claude's strength is taking a screenshot, a PDF and a text instruction in one request and processing them together.
instructions: Break the task into parts and pick a modality for each (what's better as a file, what as an image)
Assemble all inputs into one request and explicitly describe what to do with what
Example: a landing-page audit = page screenshot (Vision) + brand guide (Files) + text criteria
Ask for a single structured result, not separate answers per input
s5.validate: You can design a request where at least two modalities work toward one goal.
s5.tip: Name each input in the request text ("in the screenshot…", "in the attached PDF…") so Claude doesn't mix up sources.

s6.title: Limits, mistakes and verification
s6.why: To avoid building a broken workflow, you need to know what Claude will NOT accept directly and which modality-choice mistakes are most common.
instructions: Remember the limits: audio and video aren't accepted directly — they need preprocessing (e.g., into text)
Watch for common mistakes: converting everything to text, Vision instead of Files, context overload
Confirm the input was actually recognized — ask Claude to briefly describe what it received
Match the channel to the task: structure and text layer → file, visuals → image, fresh data → web search
